item.title: Astronomers watch a red giant star greedily devour a stellar 'Bao bun' before erupting: 'We couldn't quite believe our luck'
item.description: null Astronomers witnessed the spectacular cosmic indigestion that resulted from a red giant star that devoured a stellar Bao bun in the form of its smaller companion star. That isn't a random comparison. The cannibal star, which is 350 times bigger than the sun, is nicknamed "Big Bao," while its unfortunate companion had the nickname "Little Bao." The cute cosmic monikers come from the fact that this destructive merger event has been designated AT2025abao. A Bao bun might be a little snack for a human, but this red giant star made a real meal out of Little Bao. This cannibalistic event was tracked by a wide array of ground- and space-based telescopes, including NASA space missions NEOWISE, SPHEREx, and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), as well as the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii. The conclusion of the event AT2025abao was marked by a massive eruption witnessed in Oct. 2025 by two instruments at Caltech's Palomar Observatory: the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) and the Wide-field INfrared Transient ExploreR (WINTER). "The excitement was real," team member Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University said in a statement sent to Space.com via email. "We couldn't quite believe our luck. With detailed observations for several years before the merger, for the first time, we now have an unprecedented glimpse of the conditions that lead to such cosmic events." Reconstructing a violent cosmic collision The story of AT2025abao began when astronomers detected a bright flash in the nearby Andromeda galaxy , a region where scientists hadn't expected to see a cosmic explosion. Responding to this unexpected flash, Karambelkar and colleagues set about investigating its cause with a plethora of telescopes. This led to them seeing a slow and continuous brightening over the course of two years, They determined the cause of the flash was a rare stellar merger, the luminous red nova now designated AT2025abao. They linked this to a star called WNTR23bzdiq / WTP19aalzlk that had been observed steadily brightening since 2019 after being stable for the preceding 30 years. Thus, the team determined that at the heart of the event is a red giant, a star that puffs out to hundreds of times its original size after it runs out of hydrogen in its core. The team theorizes that Big Bao, with a mass seven times greater than the sun, expanded so rapidly and violently that it swallowed its smaller companion star. The unfortunate star, Little Bao, then spiraled into Big Bao's core in fewer than 10 orbits. "A couple of years back, we discovered a star that was gradually brightening. We took a closer look to discover a red giant, or a star that has started to expand toward the end of its life, just like our sun will one day," Karambelkar said. "Steady brightening was unusual, but even if something was stirring, no one expected to see an explosion in their lifetime, as these stars remain relatively stable for thousands of years." item.dc:creator: Robert Lea
item.content:encoded: null Astronomers witnessed the spectacular cosmic indigestion that resulted from a red giant star that devoured a stellar Bao bun in the form of its smaller companion star. That isn't a random comparison. The cannibal star, which is 350 times bigger than the sun, is nicknamed "Big Bao," while its unfortunate companion had the nickname "Little Bao." The cute cosmic monikers come from the fact that this destructive merger event has been designated AT2025abao. A Bao bun might be a little snack for a human, but this red giant star made a real meal out of Little Bao. This cannibalistic event was tracked by a wide array of ground- and space-based telescopes, including NASA space missions NEOWISE, SPHEREx, and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), as well as the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii. The conclusion of the event AT2025abao was marked by a massive eruption witnessed in Oct. 2025 by two instruments at Caltech's Palomar Observatory: the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) and the Wide-field INfrared Transient ExploreR (WINTER). "The excitement was real," team member Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University said in a statement sent to Space.com via email. "We couldn't quite believe our luck. With detailed observations for several years before the merger, for the first time, we now have an unprecedented glimpse of the conditions that lead to such cosmic events." Reconstructing a violent cosmic collision The story of AT2025abao began when astronomers detected a bright flash in the nearby Andromeda galaxy , a region where scientists hadn't expected to see a cosmic explosion. Responding to this unexpected flash, Karambelkar and colleagues set about investigating its cause with a plethora of telescopes. This led to them seeing a slow and continuous brightening over the course of two years, They determined the cause of the flash was a rare stellar merger, the luminous red nova now designated AT2025abao. They linked this to a star called WNTR23bzdiq / WTP19aalzlk that had been observed steadily brightening since 2019 after being stable for the preceding 30 years. Thus, the team determined that at the heart of the event is a red giant, a star that puffs out to hundreds of times its original size after it runs out of hydrogen in its core. The team theorizes that Big Bao, with a mass seven times greater than the sun, expanded so rapidly and violently that it swallowed its smaller companion star. The unfortunate star, Little Bao, then spiraled into Big Bao's core in fewer than 10 orbits. "A couple of years back, we discovered a star that was gradually brightening. We took a closer look to discover a red giant, or a star that has started to expand toward the end of its life, just like our sun will one day," Karambelkar said. "Steady brightening was unusual, but even if something was stirring, no one expected to see an explosion in their lifetime, as these stars remain relatively stable for thousands of years." The red nova designated AT 2025abao and its location in the Andromeda galaxy (Image credit: Palomar Observatory/ZTF/WINTER, Viraj Karambelkar) An important clue to how this cataclysmic and cannibalistic event proceeded was provided by SPHEREx in July 2025, which found that before the eruption, Big Bao was fading in optical light but brightening in infrared. This indicated that Big Bao was cooling down and spewing out dense clouds of gas and dust that were enveloping the red giant star. When Little Bao crashed into the core of Big Bao, it caused stellar material to be ejected at speeds of around 1.8 million miles per hour. This matter crashed into the envelope of gas and dust previously spewed by Big Bao, and this caused the flash of light seen on Oct. 17, 2025. The four main stages in the evolution of AT2025abao. The red giant swells out, enveloping its smaller companion star, which is then dragged into its core, ejecting material that caused a flash of light seen on Oct. 17, 2025. (Image credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Leah Hustak (STScI)) One of the final pieces of this story was provided by the JWST on Dec. 24, 2025. The powerful space telescope measured the total mass of dust and gas around Big Bao prior to the eruption since two months earlier. This helped determine that Little Bao had a mass of around 70% of the sun's mass. "It was kind of symbolic how the year was coming to an end as we managed to bring together the puzzle pieces from the story of Big and Little Bao," Karambelkar said. "But in my mind, this felt like a closure of just one chapter in a story that is just starting. We learned so much about AT2025abao, but we also learned much about conducting coordinated, multi-facility, multi-team astronomical discoveries." The team's research was published on Nov. 18 in the journal Nature.

item.title: Powerful Storm Disrupts US Thanksgiving, Leaves Over 900,000 Without Power
item.description: A powerful storm disrupted Thanksgiving celebrations for millions of Americans on Thursday, as New York’s famed Macy’s parade was postponed for the first time in its 100-year history. Heavy rain and strong winds from the “Nor-easter” battered the central and eastern United States, creating treacherous travel conditions during one of the country’s busiest holiday periods. As families were gathering for traditional holiday feasts, more than 900,000 homes and businesses were without power, with Pennsylvania, Maryland and Virginia particularly hard hit, according to tracking website PowerOutage. At airports, nearly 400 flights were cancelled, and over 2,000 were delayed in the United States, mostly in the East, figures from FlightAware showed. New York’s famed parade, which sees brightly colored balloons travel through the heart of Manhattan, was pushed back to Saturday due to what organisers said was an “abundance of caution.” Millions of people typically gather to catch a glimpse of the festivities. The only other time the parade was not held on Thanksgiving Thursday was when it was cancelled for three years during World War II. Organisers would have been only too aware of the gusting winds that wrecked the parade back in 1997 when a careening 18-foot figure of the “Cat in the Hat” toppled a lamppost, knocking one bystander unconscious. “While we are heartbroken that our parade was postponed, the safety of our partners, the safety of our participants — and spectators — is and always will be our top priority,” said Macy’s parade executive producer Will Coss. Stay Safe People brave the bad weather in the Manhattan borough of New York City on November 26, 2026. Photo by KENA BETANCUR / AFP While flooding was reported up and down the East Coast, impacts were also felt inland, with powerful gusts and inundated soil leading to trees tumbling over onto power lines and homes. Authorities in the Maryland suburbs of the US capital, worried about the impact of power outages on the water treatment network, asked nearly two million customers to conserve tap water consumption. Officials urged people to limit road travel, while several major bridges were closed due to high winds. New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill, who declared a state of emergency Wednesday over the weather, urged residents to take precautions to stay safe. “Keep your devices charged, report power outages directly to your utility provider, and stay away from downed power lines,” she wrote on X. Some people improvised to still enjoy Thanksgiving, which is traditionally marked by gathering with family around a large meal, with turkey as the centerpiece. “No electricity? No problem,” celebrity chef Jose Andres wrote on X, alongside a video of a candlelit dining room and lobsters cooking on a gas-powered stove. The East Coast disruption came as Californians also suffered weather woes this week, with massive waves battering the coast, prompting evacuations in some areas and soaking San Francisco. The

New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill, who declared a state of emergency Wednesday over the weather, urged residents to take precautions to stay safe. “Keep your devices charged, report power outages directly to your utility provider, and stay away from downed power lines,” she wrote on X. Some people improvised to still enjoy Thanksgiving, which is traditionally marked by gathering with family around a large meal, with turkey as the centerpiece. “No electricity? No problem,” celebrity chef Jose Andres wrote on X, alongside a video of a candlelit dining room and lobsters cooking on a gas-powered stove. The East Coast disruption came as Californians also suffered weather woes this week, with massive waves battering the coast, prompting evacuations in some areas and soaking San Francisco. The post Powerful Storm Disrupts US Thanksgiving, Leaves Over 900,000 Without Power appeared first on Channels Television .

item.title: AI boom leaves network operators waiting up to 18 months for kit
item.description: The AI building boom is driving up optical networking equipment prices and stretching delivery times to as much as 18 months, according to network operator RETN. RETN says that network operators and telcos are now directly competing with AI datacenters for chips and other components. As Reg readers will be aware, memory prices have soared by four or five times over the past year or so, but RETN says optical networking equipment prices have risen by around 50 percent since the start of 2026. Worse are the extended delivery times, with optical network kit that used to arrive within three months now taking 12 to 15, and some orders taking up to 18 months. This is as bad as, if not worse than, the shortages during the pandemic, when chip supply problems left network vendors unable to fulfill orders . The issue now is that because of the AI boom, demand is outpacing supplies. In its report, "AI, Connected," RETN says developers building outside established datacenter hubs may need to involve network carriers two to five years before opening. The sudden demand for network kit from hyperscalers and AI campuses is only one factor, RETN says. Raw material shortages, skilled labor shortages, energy constraints, geopolitical tensions, and logistical challenges are also compounding the issue. However, it concedes that many carriers didn't help themselves by previously postponing network upgrades to cut expenditure. That work has now become unavoidable at the worst possible time. Network diversity is now seen as a must-have, the report says. Where customers were once satisfied with two routes to long-haul destinations, they expect operators to provide four or more redundant routes now. The aim is to prevent a single failure from taking down critical services. Multiple connections are only useful protection if they avoid shared physical failure points, such as the same ducts or cable routes. A diverse circuit might cost €1,800 ($1,975) a month instead of €600 ($658), it claims, but an outage could prove far more costly. RETN also says AI datacenters are moving away from populated areas to remote locations, where access to suitable land, power and water may be easier to come by. Hyperscalers are building in the Nordics, where land is affordable, the climate is cooler, and plenty of renewable energy is available. Remote sites may lack the fiber infrastructure needed to connect them to other datacenters and customers. The Register reported on this issue earlier this year. For sites close to cities, developers often fund the fiber themselves, which adds just a few percent to the total project cost. But over longer distances, the case becomes harder to make, and carriers are understandably reluctant to build a long-haul route to serve a single remote site. Some developers are prepared to swallow the cost: RETN says a major cloud provider is exploring converting an abandoned factory in Central Europe into a large-scale server farm, despite little existing fiber in t

However, RETN's warning is that connectivity must be planned alongside power and construction, not left until the datacenter is nearly ready to open. ®

item.title: Conflicts, El Nino Worsening Hunger — UN
item.description: UN food agencies warned Friday of worsening hunger over the next six months in 16 mostly African areas, with ongoing conflicts exacerbating already dire conditions in countries like Sudan and Yemen. While armed conflict and violence are the main reasons for acute food insecurity around the globe, dramatic climate events, including El Nino, are another driver, the joint report from the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the World Food Programme (WFP) said. The Rome-based agencies listed Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia, northern Nigeria and Yemen as the areas of highest concern in its early warning about 16 “hunger hotspots” from December until May 2027. Famine remains a “plausible” risk in parts of Sudan — including North Darfur — and South Sudan, the report found. ‘Alarming levels of displacement’ The indoor cooking setup of a local food vendor, featuring large metal pots resting on industrial gas stoves. The stoves are connected directly to an orange gas cylinder running on the clean, smoke-free biogas produced by the biodigester. (Photo: Nosakhale Akhimien/Channels TV) The risk of worsening hunger comes amid a rise in “political violence events” around the world, up by more than 15 percent over the same period a year earlier, which has prompted “alarming levels of displacement in recent months”, particularly in South Sudan and Yemen. In the five countries most at risk, all repeatedly cited on the hotspot list since 2022, humanitarian assistance has declined by nearly two-thirds over the 2022-2025 period, from $5.1 billion to $2 billion. “While conflict, economic shocks, climate extremes and access constraints have remained the primary drivers of these crises, declining humanitarian resources have reduced the capacity to sustain gains and mitigate worsening conditions,” wrote FAO and WFP. While past humanitarian assistance helped avert famine, “the gains proved fragile and of limited duration: severe acute food insecurity risks — including risk of famine — re-emerged within a few years.” Also classified as a “very high concern” are Afghanistan, the Democratic Republic of Congo — which is also struggling to contend with an outbreak of Ebola — Palestine, and Haiti, where expanding gang violence has displaced 1.5 million people and disrupted humanitarian access. item.dc:creator: Channels Television
item.content:encoded: UN food agencies warned Friday of worsening hunger over the next six months in 16 mostly African areas, with ongoing conflicts exacerbating already dire conditions in countries like Sudan and Yemen. While armed conflict and violence are the main reasons for acute food insecurity around the globe, dramatic climate events, including El Nino, are another driver, the joint report from the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the World Food Programme (WFP) said. The Rome-based agencies listed Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia, northern Nigeria and Yemen as the areas of highest concern in its early warning about 16 “hunger hotspots” from December until May 2027. Famine remains a “plausible” risk in parts of Sudan — including North Darfur — and South Sudan, the report found. ‘Alarming levels of displacement’ The indoor cooking setup of a local food vendor, featuring large metal pots resting on industrial gas stoves. The stoves are connected directly to an orange gas cylinder running on the clean, smoke-free biogas produced by the biodigester. (Photo: Nosakhale Akhimien/Channels TV) The risk of worsening hunger comes amid a rise in “political violence events” around the world, up by more than 15 percent over the same period a year earlier, which has prompted “alarming levels of displacement in recent months”, particularly in South Sudan and Yemen. In the five countries most at risk, all repeatedly cited on the hotspot list since 2022, humanitarian assistance has declined by nearly two-thirds over the 2022-2025 period, from $5.1 billion to $2 billion. “While conflict, economic shocks, climate extremes and access constraints have remained the primary drivers of these crises, declining humanitarian resources have reduced the capacity to sustain gains and mitigate worsening conditions,” wrote FAO and WFP. While past humanitarian assistance helped avert famine, “the gains proved fragile and of limited duration: severe acute food insecurity risks — including risk of famine — re-emerged within a few years.” Also classified as a “very high concern” are Afghanistan, the Democratic Republic of Congo — which is also struggling to contend with an outbreak of Ebola — Palestine, and Haiti, where expanding gang violence has displaced 1.5 million people and disrupted humanitarian access. New additions to the list are Chad, Uganda, the Southern Africa region and the Central American Dry Corridor, a tropical dry forest extending from Guatemala to Costa Rica, with the latter two regions expected to be hit by the effects of El Nino, adversely affecting crops. The list also includes Mali, Myanmar and Madagascar. “Targeted humanitarian action is urgently needed to save lives and livelihoods across all hunger hotspots,” read the report. “In hotspots of highest concern, such action is critical to prevent starvation and loss of life.” Too much or little rain El Nino — the ocean warming phenomenon that is disrupting weather patterns globally, provoking devastating droughts or intense storms — is also playing a major adverse role in areas. Some 49 million more people could be pushed into acute food insecurity by the end of 2027 due to this year’s particularly intense El Nino lasting through next spring, the report estimated. “El Nino-related rainfall deficits and elevated temperatures have already contributed to crop losses in the Central American Dry Corridor and Eastern Africa, while also threatening the upcoming agricultural season in Southern Africa,” said the report, noting that wet conditions through December are expected to increase the risk of floods in areas of Eastern Africa. In the Gaza Strip, meanwhile, “winter rains and localized flooding could worsen conditions for displaced households — damaging inadequate shelters and further disrupting essential services and humanitarian operations,” it read. Anticipatory measures such as adapted seeds, better protection of livestock and water supplies, along with timely assistance, can make a difference. But a FAO-WFP plan faces a funding shortfall of $125 million, the agencies said. The post Conflicts, El Nino Worsening Hunger — UN appeared first on Channels Television .

Apple, Beats, Soundcore, Sony, Nothing, and other major brands are offering some of the best prices we’ve seen on many of their products, whether you’re on a tight sub-$100 budget or willing to spend more (but still want a great deal). We’re seeing some surprisingly great sale prices, especially on noise-canceling earbuds like the AirPods Pro 3 and Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro . item.title: 2027: Lokpobiri rallies Bayelsa West for Tinubu’s re-election
item.description: Minister of State for Petroleum Resources (Oil), Senator Heineken Lokpobiri, has urged voters in Bayelsa West Senatorial District to support President Bola Tinubu’s re-election and all All Progressives Congress (APC) candidates in the 2027 general elections. Lokpobiri made the appeal on Thursday, November 26, during a pre-campaign sensitisation exercise organised by the Bayelsa West APC Campaign Directorate in Aleibiri, Ebedebiri and Agbere communities. Addressing party members, stakeholders and residents, the minister urged them to remain committed to the APC, saying sustained support for the party was necessary to consolidate the reforms and transformation being pursued by the Tinubu administration under its Renewed Hope Agenda. He said Tinubu had demonstrated the courage, vision and determination to reposition the country through what he described as bold reforms and purposeful leadership. “President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has remained committed to delivering on his Renewed Hope mandate and transforming our dear nation. The progress being made requires our collective support and commitment to ensure that the gains are sustained. We must therefore give him another mandate in 2027,” he said. The minister also called on the people to support all APC candidates, stressing that political unity, grassroots mobilisation and collective participation would be crucial to the party’s prospects in the elections. “I urge the good people of Bayelsa West to stand firmly with President Tinubu and all APC candidates. This is the time to consolidate our structures, strengthen our grassroots engagement and work together towards victory,” he added. The sensitisation exercise, according to the organisers, was part of the party’s efforts to strengthen grassroots mobilisation, encourage peaceful political participation and build support structures across Bayelsa West ahead of the 2027 general elections. item.title: 2027: Kwankwaso accuses Kano governor of plot to tarnish his image
item.description: Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso, vice-presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), has accused Kano State Governor, Abba Yusuf, of allegedly orchestrating a campaign to tarnish his reputation ahead of the 2027 general elections. Kwankwaso made the allegation in a statement issued on Friday, expressing concern over what he described as the alleged use of anti-corruption institutions, particularly the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC), for political purposes. The former Kano State governor questioned the motives behind what he characterised as attempts to damage his public image, alleging that the anti-corruption agency was being drawn into political activities. He expressed concern that institutions established to fight corruption could be used to settle political scores, particularly as political activities gather momentum ahead of the 2027 elections. However, the allegations against Governor Yusuf remain claims by Kwankwaso and would require an independent response from the governor or his representatives. The post 2027: Kwankwaso accuses Kano governor of plot to tarnish his image appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Shettima, Akande, Saraki, traditional rulers attend Adeleke’s inauguration
item.description: By Shina Abubakar, Osogbo Vice-President Kashim Shettima on Friday led prominent personalities to the second-term inauguration of Osun State Governor, Ademola Adeleke, held at the Osogbo Township Stadium. Adeleke was re-elected governor on August 15, 2026, defeating the All Progressives Congress (APC) candidate, Bola Oyebamiji, by more than 60,000 votes. The inauguration, which was ongoing at the time of filing this report, attracted several political figures, including APC National Leader, Chief Bisi Akande; former Senate President, Bukola Saraki; and former APC National Secretary, Senator Iyiola Omisore. Also in attendance were former Osun State Deputy Governor, Benedict Alabi; the Olubadan of Ibadan, Oba Rashidi Ladoja; the Soun of Ogbomoso, Oba Ghandi Olaoye; and the Ataoja of Osogbo, Oba Jimoh Olanipekun, among other traditional rulers. Captains of industry, academics, politicians and other dignitaries were also present at the ceremony. The post Shettima, Akande, Saraki, traditional rulers attend Adeleke’s inauguration appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: 2027: Emerging opposition coalition comprises displaced politicians — Lagos APC
item.description: By Olasunkanmi Akoni The Lagos State chapter of the All Progressives Congress (APC) has criticised ongoing merger and coalition talks among opposition figures ahead of the 2027 general elections, describing the emerging alliance as an association of “internally displaced politicians” driven by personal grievances rather than a coherent vision for governance. The Lagos APC spokesman, Seye Oladejo, who made the remark on Friday, questioned the ideological consistency and sincerity of the political actors seeking to unite against President Bola Tinubu in 2027. According to Oladejo, the emerging alliance comprises former power brokers, ex-officeholders and frustrated aspirants who previously benefited from or helped shape the same political establishments they now criticise. He maintained that the coalition lacked a unified policy framework on critical national issues, including economic management, energy reforms, foreign exchange policy and national security. “What is being marketed to Nigerians as a formidable opposition coalition increasingly looks like an assembly of politically displaced persons, disgruntled power brokers, frustrated presidential aspirants and former beneficiaries of the very political establishments they now denounce,” the Lagos APC spokesman said. Reacting to another round of opposition consultations scheduled for Monday, Oladejo dismissed the repeated meetings as “political motion without movement”. He argued that bringing prominent political figures together under one roof did not automatically translate into grassroots electoral structures or administrative competence. Oladejo further contended that opposition rhetoric had become excessively focused on opposing Tinubu rather than presenting a credible alternative blueprint for governance. While acknowledging that the economic reforms introduced by the Tinubu administration had brought difficult adjustments for households and businesses, the Lagos APC maintained that the 2027 election would be determined by verifiable performance records, policy continuity and organisational strength rather than what it described as a “coalition of grievances”. The post 2027: Emerging opposition coalition comprises displaced politicians — Lagos APC appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: GTA in Istanbul? Meet the game developers bringing virtual crime chaos to their home cities
item.description: From Helsinki to Istanbul, independent developers are putting Grand Theft Auto-style action on their home streets, and without billion-dollar budgets. They tell us how they do it Like most kids who shouldn’t have been playing Grand Theft Auto III in 2001, Eamonn Swayah imagined a version of Rockstar Games’ groundbreaking criminal sandbox set in his own back yard. In his case, that was a Manchester council estate, complete with local accents, driving on the left, and plenty of ways to hustle. He didn’t know it, but swapping the game’s facsimile of early 2000s New York City for a different setting was an idea he shared with many watchful game developers. Rockstar’s 3D open world template, it turned out, could be plonked in just about any location, so long as it had people and enough cars to run them over with. After GTA III attracted immense commercial success (and controversy), dozens of copycats and spiritual sequels hit the market throughout the 00s and 2010s. Gamers had a pithy name for them: “GTA clones”. Continue reading...

item.title: 2027 Election:​‌‍‍‍‍⁠⁠‍⁠​‍‌‌​‍‍‌​ INEC procures 57,000 new BVAS devices
item.description: The Chairman of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), Prof. Joash Amupitan, says the commission has procured 57,000 new BVAS for the 2027 general elections. Prof. Amupitan disclosed this on Thursday during a sensitisation seminar by the Diocese of Abuja, Anglican Communion, on Civil and Political Education with the theme “Why Your Vote Still Matters” Represented by the Deputy Director, Voter Education and Publicity, Mr Wilfred Ifogah, Prof. Amupitan said that the commission had also reduced the threshold from 1,250 to 850 voters per machine and cleaned the register through biometric audit. He said that with 51 days to the Jan. 16, 2027, presidential and National Assembly elections, civic responsibility must not be outsourced. Amupitan said INEC would on Saturday conduct a nationwide mock accreditation exercise in two polling units per ward to test upgrades ahead of 2027. According to him, over 10.77 million new registrants were recorded during the Continuous Voter Registration, while over 1.6 million invalid records were removed, bringing the verified register to over 100 million voters, including 232,658 persons with disabilities. He said INEC had also upgraded its Result Viewing Portal, IReV, with automated checks for over-voting and arithmetic consistency on Form EC8A before transmission. The INEC boss urged citizens to resist vote buying, divisive politics and inflammatory language, noting that Sections 95, 96 and 97 of the Electoral Act 2026 prescribe stiff penalties for electoral violence and hate speech. Also speaking, a legal practitioner, Mr Emeka Etiaba, SAN, said over-judicialisation of elections was eroding public confidence. Etiaba said trust is earned, not commanded, stressing that INEC and the judiciary must deliver credible processes in 2027 to restore confidence. He noted that technicalities, poor petition drafting and non-justiciable innovations often deny determination of cases on merit, leaving a few judges to decide outcomes involving thousands of voters. He said innovations such as AI validation on IReV, though laudable administratively, must be backed by law to be enforceable in court. Speaking at the event, the Primate of the Church of Nigeria, Anglican Communion, Most Rev. Henry Ndukuba, urged Nigerians, especially youths, to actively participate in the 2027 general elections. According to him, their votes remain critical to deepening democracy and national development. Prof. Amupitan disclosed this on Thursday during a sensitisation seminar by the Diocese of Abuja, Anglican Communion, on Civil and Political Education with the theme “Why Your Vote Still Matters” Represented by the Deputy Director, Voter Education and Publicity, Mr Wilfred Ifogah, Prof. Amupitan said that the commission had also reduced the threshold from 1,250 to 850 voters per machine and cleaned the register through biometric audit. He said that with 51 days to the Jan. 16, 2027, presidential and National Assembly elections, civic responsibility must not be outsourced. Amupitan said INEC would on Saturday conduct a nationwide mock accreditation exercise in two polling units per ward to test upgrades ahead of 2027. According to him, over 10.77 million new registrants were recorded during the Continuous Voter Registration, while over 1.6 million invalid records were removed, bringing the verified register to over 100 million voters, including 232,658 persons with disabilities. He said INEC had also upgraded its Result Viewing Portal, IReV, with automated checks for over-voting and arithmetic consistency on Form EC8A before transmission. The INEC boss urged citizens to resist vote buying, divisive politics and inflammatory language, noting that Sections 95, 96 and 97 of the Electoral Act 2026 prescribe stiff penalties for electoral violence and hate speech. Also speaking, a legal practitioner, Mr Emeka Etiaba, SAN, said over-judicialisation of elections was eroding public confidence. Etiaba said trust is earned, not commanded, stressing that INEC and the judiciary must deliver credible processes in 2027 to restore confidence. He noted that technicalities, poor petition drafting and non-justiciable innovations often deny determination of cases on merit, leaving a few judges to decide outcomes involving thousands of voters. He said innovations such as AI validation on IReV, though laudable administratively, must be backed by law to be enforceable in court. Speaking at the event, the Primate of the Church of Nigeria, Anglican Communion, Most Rev. Henry Ndukuba, urged Nigerians, especially youths, to actively participate in the 2027 general elections. According to him, their votes remain critical to deepening democracy and national development. The News Agency of Nigeria reports that the seminar is part of activities marking the 37th anniversary of the diocese and Carnival for Christ 2026. Ndukuba said the church organised the seminar to sensitise citizens on their civic responsibility ahead of the polls, and the 2027 electioneering campaigns were already underway, with general elections scheduled for January 2027. He said the church deemed it important to engage stakeholders in the electoral process to educate citizens on the need to make informed decisions. “Most of our citizens have lost confidence in our democratic processes. The church was committed to mobilising Nigerians to register, verify their names when INEC publishes the voters’ list and vote on Election Day.” According to him, politics concerns the distribution and management of national resources, care for citizens and opportunities for young people; hence the need for all Nigerians to be involved. “Nigeria is for all of us, no matter your religion or background. We have the right to determine who leads us,” Ndukuba said. On her part, Senior Manager, YIAGA Africa, Ms Safiya Bichi, urged young people to move beyond social media activism to actual voting and mobilisation. “Whether you turn out to vote or not, you have made a decision. Votes are decided by those who turn out,” she said. Bichi said if votes were not valuable, politicians would not buy them, urging young Christians and urban voters to participate actively. NAN also reports that the Diocese of Abuja is marking 37 years of pastoral ministry, community service and moral witness, with the carnival focusing on faith, citizenship and responsible participation in national life. item.title: British social security system techies yank services offline following 'cyber incident'
item.description: The UK's Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) has taken some services offline after detecting a "cyber incident," but says regular benefit and pension payments are unaffected. The department announced the precautionary shutdown on Friday morning. "We have taken some DWP online services offline as a precaution after we identified a cyber incident affecting our systems," it said. "We are working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre (GC3) to investigate and to bring services back online as quickly as possible and to minimize any disruption. "Regular benefit and pension payments are not affected and will be paid as normal. If an online service you need is unavailable, please try again later. As always, we will never message you to ask for bank details or ask you to click on links." The Register contacted both the DWP and NCSC for more information. The DWP declined to comment beyond the statement issued publicly. GC3 coordinates responses to incidents affecting government. The Government Cyber Unit leads the wider Government Cyber Action Plan, backed by more than £210 million. It is led by the government CISO, Bella Powell. Officials have not commented on any of the usual details one would expect from a cyber incident disclosure, including the specific services that were downed, when they are expected to return, or whether any data is thought to be compromised, even at this early stage. The UK government has also been criticized recently for investing heavily in AI cyber defenses, while the issue of legacy and aging IT continues to be neglected in the background. It announced at the end of October that it was throwing £130 million at AI cyber defense technology , as part of a wider £600 million cross-government AI spending spree announced by the Treasury. ExfilSquad recently claimed to have stolen around 607,000 records from the Department for Education and another 114,000 from the Police National Legal Database. ®

item.title: Can Borussia Dortmund finally end their title wait? Three big questions for Bundesliga leaders
item.description: Niko Kovac’s team lead the way and, with Bayern Munich wounded, have a golden chance to be German champions for the first time in 15 years Borussia Dortmund’s dreams have a habit of becoming nightmares, like when they somehow handed Bayern Munich the Bundesliga title on the final day of the 2022-23 season. Or when an 89th-minute Arjen Robben goal won the 2013 Champions League final for the same opponents. Whenever Dortmund suffer heartbreak, it usually involves Bayern. As things stand, however, Niko Kovac’s side hold a two-point lead over Bayern at the top of the Bundesliga. item.title: Questions about Tinubu’s identity come up anytime he’s about to win election — Fashola
item.description: Former Lagos State Governor Babatunde Fashola has dismissed renewed questions about President Bola Tinubu’s background and identity, saying the controversies resurface whenever the president is on the verge of winning an election. Fashola described the questions as needless distractions, insisting that Tinubu had met the constitutional requirements to contest the presidency and that Nigerians had already settled the matter through their votes. He said the controversy had persisted for more than two decades but had not stopped Tinubu from winning elections, expressing confidence that the president would secure another victory in 2027. Fashola spoke in an interview with ARISE News while responding to questions about the perceived secrecy surrounding Tinubu’s background and identity. “I think that these matters have carried on for all of 20-something years. So, every time he’s at the threshold of winning an election, these issues come, and you know what always happens: he wins,” he said. “So history is about to repeat itself again. He’s going to win. These are needless distractions. They don’t answer a fundamental question. And I’ve said about minimum qualification. He has met it,” the former governor added. Fashola questioned the relevance of the controversies to Nigerians, saying opposition politicians should focus on issues that would improve the lives of citizens rather than repeatedly raising questions about Tinubu’s background. “The question I will focus upon if I were those fragmented opposition is how does this help the people whose mandate I want? It doesn’t help them,” he said. The former minister of works also argued that some of the issues had previously been subjected to legal proceedings and investigations, including during the 1999 political period and the last presidential election. Drawing on his experience as a legal practitioner, Fashola said there was a need to allow an end to prolonged disputes, invoking the legal principle that litigation must eventually come to a conclusion. “I believe parts of this were litigated in the last election. They were litigated in 1999. It was the subject of a House investigation in that period. You keep referring to my other life as a legal practitioner, there’s a principle in that life. There’s something we say, a principle that there must be an end to litigation. It’s enough,” he said. Fashola said Nigerians had moved on from the controversy, citing Tinubu’s victory in the 2023 presidential election as evidence, and predicted that voters would reaffirm their position in 2027. “They pursue it at their own choice, but I think the Nigerian people have left that subject behind. They have left it behind with their votes in 2023. They will reaffirm it in 2027,” he said. The post Questions about Tinubu’s identity come up anytime he’s about to win election — Fashola appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: New Scientist Book Club: How urine changed the course of human history
item.description: A detail from Joseph Wright’s 1771 painting The Alchemist Discovering Phosphorus, showing Henning Brand in 1669 Science History Images/Alamy Imagine you could boil the development of science down to a single ingredient. A magical, mystical compound that transformed human history. Of course, science doesn’t work that way; even if breakthroughs shift the paradigm of our understanding, discovery doesn’t progress like a tech tree in a computer game, but as an interweaving tapestry of complementary and competing ideas and experimentation. Theories can bubble under the surface for centuries, overlooked because of politics or failure to realise their implications, while innovations can emerge from taking an idea in one industry and transplanting it to another. But, for a moment, try and picture what just one such ingredient could be. What would you pick? For centuries, in medieval Europe, alchemists quested for the “Philosopher’s Stone” that would finally help them achieve their dreams of transmutation. It was a search doomed to failure from the very beginning. And yet, a far better idea was under their noses – or, rather, their underpants – the entire time. My pick? Urine has a strong case for being the most transformative substance in human history. Free newsletter Sign up to Book Club Sign up to newsletter The development of civilisation was built on chemistry. It required the first chemical reaction we mastered – fire – to keep us warm, cook our food and smelt ores. But leatherwork played an equally key role. Urine is a source of urea, which bacteria can break down into ammonia, granting early humans easy access to a base that could soften organic matter and tan hides. Across the world, leatherwork became the cornerstone of survival for every civilisation, from the Americas to Europe, Africa and Asia: even cultures that didn’t develop a bronze age, such as the Aztec, or skipped it entirely, as seen in Sub-Saharan Africa, relied on leatherwork for clothes, structures, industry and commerce. Advertisement If the power of pee helped build civilisation, it would go on to be foundational in its upkeep. In ancient Rome, urine was so useful for laundries to keep togas whiter-than-white that Emperor Vespasian levied a tax on draining urinals. When his son complained, Vespasian’s response was blunt: pecunia non olet , money doesn’t stink. Part of the funds were used to build the Colosseum in Rome, today recognised as one of the wonders of the world. The magic of urine filtered into what would become chemical science, too. Cheimeia , the artisanal trade secrets and recipes found in Alexandria, Egypt, that would later give rise to alchemy, recognised the value of urine. In the Leiden Papyrus X , part of a cluster of the only original manuscripts on alchemy’s origins we still have, you can find a recipe for faking gold using polysulfides. item.dc:creator: Kit Chapman
item.content:encoded: A detail from Joseph Wright’s 1771 painting The Alchemist Discovering Phosphorus, showing Henning Brand in 1669 Science History Images/Alamy Imagine you could boil the development of science down to a single ingredient. A magical, mystical compound that transformed human history. Of course, science doesn’t work that way; even if breakthroughs shift the paradigm of our understanding, discovery doesn’t progress like a tech tree in a computer game, but as an interweaving tapestry of complementary and competing ideas and experimentation. Theories can bubble under the surface for centuries, overlooked because of politics or failure to realise their implications, while innovations can emerge from taking an idea in one industry and transplanting it to another. But, for a moment, try and picture what just one such ingredient could be. What would you pick? For centuries, in medieval Europe, alchemists quested for the “Philosopher’s Stone” that would finally help them achieve their dreams of transmutation. It was a search doomed to failure from the very beginning. And yet, a far better idea was under their noses – or, rather, their underpants – the entire time. My pick? Urine has a strong case for being the most transformative substance in human history. Free newsletter Sign up to Book Club Sign up to newsletter The development of civilisation was built on chemistry. It required the first chemical reaction we mastered – fire – to keep us warm, cook our food and smelt ores. But leatherwork played an equally key role. Urine is a source of urea, which bacteria can break down into ammonia, granting early humans easy access to a base that could soften organic matter and tan hides. Across the world, leatherwork became the cornerstone of survival for every civilisation, from the Americas to Europe, Africa and Asia: even cultures that didn’t develop a bronze age, such as the Aztec, or skipped it entirely, as seen in Sub-Saharan Africa, relied on leatherwork for clothes, structures, industry and commerce. Advertisement If the power of pee helped build civilisation, it would go on to be foundational in its upkeep. In ancient Rome, urine was so useful for laundries to keep togas whiter-than-white that Emperor Vespasian levied a tax on draining urinals. When his son complained, Vespasian’s response was blunt: pecunia non olet , money doesn’t stink. Part of the funds were used to build the Colosseum in Rome, today recognised as one of the wonders of the world. The magic of urine filtered into what would become chemical science, too. Cheimeia , the artisanal trade secrets and recipes found in Alexandria, Egypt, that would later give rise to alchemy, recognised the value of urine. In the Leiden Papyrus X , part of a cluster of the only original manuscripts on alchemy’s origins we still have, you can find a recipe for faking gold using polysulfides. In it, the recipe suggests using the “urine of a small child”, although today our understanding of the chemical reaction that creates the effect means we know water is a better alternative. The 28 best popular science books of 2026 From space-time to saunas, here are the very best popular science books published this year that you should be adding to your Christmas list Fast-forward a thousand years, and the mass use of urine was commonplace around the world. It was still used for laundry and leatherwork, but was now also part of the burgeoning gunpowder industry. One of the key ingredients of this game-changing superweapon, the origins of which lie in Chinese herbal medicine, is saltpetre, or potassium nitrate. This was gathered from nitre beds, stinking manure heaps mixed with potash and mortar, all moistened with urine to claim the nitrates. This method, used from Europe to Japan, continued well into the 19th century; during the US Civil War, the Confederacy was using urine to keep its guns firing. But perhaps urine’s greatest contribution came from alchemy. By the 17th century, just as the printing press and improvements in lenses and glassware had finally begun to usher in the scientific method, the old practices and beliefs that blended experiment, philosophy, religion and misunderstanding of the ancient world had their greatest triumph. In 1669, an alchemist in Hamburg, Hennig Brand, was searching for the philosopher’s stone using 1500 gallons of fermented urine he had collected in his basement. To Brand’s astonishment, the concentrated urine at the heart of his experiment began to glow. Brand kept his accomplishment secret for years, but unable to take the next step and turn metals into gold, he eventually sold the recipe to a friend and the discovery was shared with the world. Brand hadn’t performed a magic trick, but isolated phosphorus – the first chemical element to be discovered in modern times. Today, urine still plays a critical role around the world, particularly in medicine, where it is a source of biomarkers used in diagnostic tests, and was even the original source of drugs such as human chorionic gonadotropin and follicle-stimulating hormone for fertility treatment. As Emperor Vespasian said almost 2000 years ago, money doesn’t stink – and nor do the benefits of the amber liquid we all produce every day. Kit Chapman is the author of The Age of Alchemy , the December read for the New Scientist Book Club. Sign up for the club here , and join the discussion on Discord here . item.title: Read an extract from The Age of Alchemy by Kit Chapman
item.description: The New Scientist Book Club is reading The Age of Alchemy in December “ A handful of lime and another of sulfur in fine powder. Place them in a vessel containing strong vinegar or the urine of a small child. Heat it from below, until the liquid appears like blood. Advertisement Decant this properly, and use. ” Unknown, Leiden Papyrus X , c. 300 CE In 1827, amid the dark, silent balm of an Egyptian night, a graverobber pulled a treasure from the sands. At first, the raider was frustrated; scavenging the tombs near Thebes, he had hoped to uncover a priceless heirloom, or a nugget of gold that would sparkle with lustre in the starlight. Instead, he had found only a clutch of rolled scrolls, made of papyrus and sealed against the elements. For a moment, he considered casting the documents aside and leaving them for the desert. Then greed got the better of him. Westerners loved all things Egyptian, he reasoned. Since the French had arrived with Napoleon, the new field of “Egyptology” had swept the continent, capturing the imagination of scholars and the wealthy. It was almost as popular as the new science of “chemistry”. Surely, if he took his find to the market, he’d find some gullible fool willing to buy it. The buyer’s name was Jean d’Anastasy, and he was anything but a fool. Born in Greece as the son of a Damascus merchant who had won and lost his fortune in the Napoleonic Wars, d’Anastasy had used his family’s connections to set himself up as a grain merchant in Alexandria, before scheming his way into being named the local Consul General for Sweden and Norway. Free newsletter Sign up to Book Club Sign up to newsletter When d’Anastasy wasn’t trading – or rescuing enslaved girls during the Greek War of Independence against the Ottoman Empire – he ran a side-hustle, “procuring” relics from Ancient Egypt and selling them to the salons of Europe: statues to the British Museum in London; rings and jewels to the Louvre in Paris; even a pair of sphinxes that still sit on the banks of the Neva River in St Petersburg. He quickly saw the value of the papers, paid for them, and shipped them back to Europe. Some went to Stockholm, and some to Leiden University in the Netherlands. Among the Leiden trove was one of the most remarkable finds in history: a papyrus scroll with a list of recipes, each with crystal-clear instructions written in Greek. While we have damaged cuneiform tablets and later copies of older works, the Leiden Papyrus X , written around 300 CE, is the oldest surviving alchemy book in history. It is a guide for Egyptian artisans to create wondrous riches, seemingly out of nothing. There are methods on how to polish silverware, cheap alternatives for making knock-off purple robes, and how to create gold lettering by mixing saffron and tortoise bile. item.content:encoded: The New Scientist Book Club is reading The Age of Alchemy in December “ A handful of lime and another of sulfur in fine powder. Place them in a vessel containing strong vinegar or the urine of a small child. Heat it from below, until the liquid appears like blood. Advertisement Decant this properly, and use. ” Unknown, Leiden Papyrus X , c. 300 CE In 1827, amid the dark, silent balm of an Egyptian night, a graverobber pulled a treasure from the sands. The buyer’s name was Jean d’Anastasy, and he was anything but a fool. Free newsletter Sign up to Book Club Sign up to newsletter When d’Anastasy wasn’t trading – or rescuing enslaved girls during the Greek War of Independence against the Ottoman Empire – he ran a side-hustle, “procuring” relics from Ancient Egypt and selling them to the salons of Europe: statues to the British Museum in London; rings and jewels to the Louvre in Paris; even a pair of sphinxes that still sit on the banks of the Neva River in St Petersburg. He quickly saw the value of the papers, paid for them, and shipped them back to Europe. Some went to Stockholm, and some to Leiden University in the Netherlands. Among the Leiden trove was one of the most remarkable finds in history: a papyrus scroll with a list of recipes, each with crystal-clear instructions written in Greek. While we have damaged cuneiform tablets and later copies of older works, the Leiden Papyrus X , written around 300 CE, is the oldest surviving alchemy book in history. It is a guide for Egyptian artisans to create wondrous riches, seemingly out of nothing. There are methods on how to polish silverware, cheap alternatives for making knock-off purple robes, and how to create gold lettering by mixing saffron and tortoise bile. These are all real instructions, and all recipes that work (even if, today, there are cheaper ways to get the same result). Among them is the greatest secret in alchemy. It’s called the “invention of sulfur water” and is the recipe at the start of this chapter. Sulfur and lime (calcium oxide, not the fruit) are gardening supplies that you can buy in a hardware store, and if you don’t have a small child that needs a wee to hand, strong vinegar from the supermarket will work just as well. While you shouldn’t try this at home, the result, after you heat the mix for an hour, is a red-brown goop and a kitchen that reeks of rotten eggs. These are calcium polysulfides, making up lime sulfur. It’s a nasty substance – an alkali that can cause skin irritation and even blindness if you get it in your eyes. Today, we use this for pest control, but in ancient times it was how you created gold. Well, the appearance of gold. Once you’ve got your “sulfur water”, any metal object submersed – a coin, nail or paperclip – will gain a thin, yellowy film coating. The Leiden Papyrus X isn’t just the oldest alchemy book in history. It’s a tried-and-tested guide for tricksters. We may not know who wrote the document, but we do know that if you had walked into the author’s workshop 1,700 years ago, you’d have been swindled. Or that’s how it seems. The truth, as we’ll learn, is that something else was going on that’s even more fascinating. But we’re getting ahead of ourselves. The 28 best popular science books of 2026 From space-time to saunas, here are the very best popular science books published this year that you should be adding to your Christmas list The Leiden Papyrus X isn’t what most people think of when they picture alchemy. We think of it as a pseudoscience, a blend of religious beliefs, ancient superstition and gilded dreams, with only the occasional glimpse of something that might work underneath. If you subscribe to the traditional view, this is the best you can hope for when it comes to studying any chemistry earlier than about 1650. Before the Enlightenment, there were only wizards, witches and wishful thinking. Then suddenly, whoosh , in a flash of gunpowder, a crackle of electricity and bubbling fizz from a test tube, a new science arrived to change our world. This book turns that idea on its head. No one person created chemistry, and even if they had, it certainly wouldn’t have been some white European in a powdered wig. Chemistry didn’t appear overnight and there is no one moment when it came into existence. It was a gradual transformation that built on millennia of knowledge. Choosing to ignore chemistry during the Age of Alchemy does a disservice to thousands of men and women, across the world, who guided us from the first campfire to the modern age. This book is divided into three parts. In the first, we look at how early chemistry worked, from the Stone Age up to the emergence of alchemy, and how it set the basic principles for what alchemy, and later chemistry, would become. In the second, we go on a trip around the world. Practically every history of alchemy just focuses on the western traditions – mainly because they are the best studied. But we’re going to look at what was happening with chemistry in the Islamic world, China, the Indian subcontinent and even the Americas. Some of this is alchemy, and some of it isn’t, but it all plays a role in the tapestry of science. Finally, the third section returns to Europe, where we’ll look at how alchemy changed (or, to use the alchemical term, transmuted), over the course of several hundred years, into the science we know today. My journey has led to travels across six continents and taken me on adventures through deserts and jungles, tombs and tomes, and some of our most fabled cities. I have explored old roads and met the researchers busy paving new ones. The result is a story that is both a mirror to progress and a love letter to science, one that offers a glimpse into the past and shows how it all connects to our daily lives, often in surprising and roundabout ways. Chemistry is everywhere and is linked to everything. It is painfully human. It is filled with our mistakes, beliefs and hubris. It showcases our noble endeavours, destructive potential and indomitable spirit. And it allows us to appreciate how science, whether through petty rivalries, oppression and colonisation, or religious fervour, has always been political. © Kit Chapman This is an extract from The Age of Alchemy by Kit Chapman, the December read for the New Scientist Book Club. item.title: Royal Navy orders £142M in minehunting drones from US supplier
item.description: Britain's Royal Navy is investing £142 million ($185 million) in underwater drones to tackle sea mines, but the contract has gone to an American defense supplier. The Ministry of Defence (MoD) says that the UK's ability to protect vital sea routes will be strengthened through the procurement of these Uncrewed Underwater Vehicles (UUVs). These will form part of the Royal Navy's move toward a " Hybrid Navy " comprising a mix of crewed, uncrewed, and autonomous platforms in order to meet future challenges. The UUV selected for the job is the REMUS 620 , built by Huntington Ingalls Industries (HII), the largest military shipbuilding company in the United States. HII has a facility at Portchester, on the south coast of England, but is still a US-owned company. We asked the MoD how the award fits its pledge to prioritize buying British wherever possible, and what share of the contract's value will support UK industry. The contract includes HII's Sea Launcher automated launch and recovery systems and will bring support services previously delivered overseas to the UK. HII says it will support 15 jobs, while the MoD identifies Portchester among the locations benefiting. HII says this is the largest international order in its 25-year history of supplying uncrewed systems. The MoD has previously acquired REMUS 100, REMUS 300, and REMUS 600 vehicles for mine countermeasure operations. The new vehicles will locate sea mines to support clearance operations and help keep shipping routes open. By using drones to comb a body of water for explosive devices, the Royal Navy's crews can be kept a safe distance from any potential immediate threat. Traditionally, this work has been conducted by specialist crewed ships such as the Hunt class or Sandown class , but these are being retired from service in favor of uncrewed systems. The Royal Navy also operates SWEEP , an uncrewed boat towing equipment that mimics a ship's magnetic, acoustic, and electric signatures to trigger mines from a safe distance. The new REMUS underwater vehicles can be sent ahead of other vessels to search beneath the surface, making minehunting operations safer, faster and more flexible, according to the MoD. "This investment strengthens our ability to protect freedom of navigation, which is critical to our security and our economy," said Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP. Like others in the portfolio, REMUS 620 resembles a naval torpedo. It is capable of operating at depths of 600 meters and has an endurance of up to 110 hours on a single mission. The drones will be integrated with SeeTrack and Neptune software developed by SeeByte in the UK, which is already used by the Royal Navy. In trials announced in October 2025, a REMUS 620 demonstrated launch and recovery using a submerged test fixture replicating a Virginia-class submarine's torpedo tube. The work could enable submarines to deploy and retrieve underwater drones on future missions. ®

item.title: People who opposed Tinubu now work with him — Fashola
item.description: Former Lagos State Governor Babatunde Fashola has said President Bola Tinubu’s ability to retain former allies and reconcile political opponents demonstrates his capacity to manage Nigeria’s diversity and build consensus. Fashola said politicians who opposed Tinubu in the past had now joined forces with him, describing the president’s ability to bring former adversaries together as evidence of his leadership and capacity to work with others. He spoke in an interview with ARISE News while responding to why Nigerians should give Tinubu another four years in office. The former minister of works said voters should assess the presidential candidates based on their relationships with people they previously worked with, arguing that the ability to sustain working relationships through difficult periods was an important measure of leadership. “The three main presidential candidates today share one trait in common. They all started as governors. One of them didn’t take office, but he was already a governor-elect, Vice President Atiku Abubakar. Where are all the people who worked with them today? That’s a job reference question for those who want to vote,” Fashola said. He asked why many of those who worked with Tinubu during his time as Lagos governor had remained with him, while political associates of other candidates had moved on. “Where are all the people who worked with these people? Why is it only President Tinubu that has all those who worked with him still with him? And they were with him for 16 years or so out of office when he wasn’t a president. That’s a very good answer to the question,” he said. Fashola said the loyalty of Tinubu’s associates reflected his ability to work with others and manage disagreements without abandoning relationships, adding that such qualities were important for a president leading a country with diverse interests. “It shows an ability to work with others. If you are going to get entrusted with managing Nigeria’s diverse family, you must be able to work in a team, and you don’t just get up and jump away when there is crisis in the fold,” he said. He contrasted Tinubu’s political experience with that of other candidates, saying the president remained in the APC despite internal crises, while others left the parties through which they rose to prominence. “There was crisis in the APC. He didn’t leave the party. The others have left the parties that brought them to prominence,” Fashola said. The former governor further argued that Tinubu had expanded his political alliances by bringing former opponents into his fold, including those who once strongly opposed him. “All the people who opposed Tinubu when he used to be called the last man standing. All of them are now working with him. Not just those who worked with him before; those who oppose him are now working with him,” he said. item.title: From fuel subsidy return to Ajaokuta revival; Atiku’s 2027 promises so far
item.description: Former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar has promised to restore petrol and electricity subsidies, tackle insecurity, create jobs and revive key infrastructure projects if elected president in 2027. The African Democratic Congress (ADC) presidential candidate has made the pledges at campaign rallies in Sokoto, Bauchi, Yobe and Kogi states, while presenting his proposed policies as measures to reduce the cost of living and improve economic conditions. At the ADC presidential campaign flag-off in Sokoto on November 4 , Atiku promised to restore petrol subsidy, reopen Nigeria’s land borders to encourage trade and tackle insecurity, including kidnapping, banditry and terrorism. He also pledged to reduce the cost of pilgrimage for Muslim and Christian faithful. Atiku said restoring petrol subsidy would help reduce transportation costs and ease the burden of rising prices of essential goods. He also argued that reopening the land borders would benefit farmers, traders and transport operators by stimulating cross-border commerce. At a rally in Bauchi State on November 14, Atiku extended his subsidy promise to electricity, saying he would restore both petroleum and electricity subsidies if elected. He also pledged to strengthen security, particularly in the North-East, resume oil exploration in the Kolmani field and continue the Mambilla Hydroelectric Power Project. “I will restore electricity subsidies. I also promise to restore security in the North-East sub-region and the country at large. I further promise to continue oil exploration activities in Kolmani so that we can have additional sources of revenue,” he said at the Bauchi rally. At a campaign rally in Yobe State on November 15, Atiku again promised to restore petrol and electricity subsidies, while pledging to address insecurity and create employment opportunities for young Nigerians. “Let me assure you that once I am elected president in 2027, I will bring back the fuel subsidy,” he said, adding that he would also restore electricity subsidy. He further promised that his administration would work to ensure peace returned to Yobe and other parts of the country, and that young Nigerians would have access to employment opportunities. In Kogi State on November 24 , Atiku campaigned on an “Affordable Life” message, promising to reduce fuel costs, support local production and improve Nigerians’ purchasing power. He said his proposals were aimed at easing the pressure on households, workers and small businesses. At the rally in Lokoja, he also pledged to revive and complete the Ajaokuta Steel Mill through foreign investment, without relying on government funding for the project. He promised to continue the Baro Port project by dredging the River Niger to enable the port to serve other states and create employment opportunities. “I want to promise you here today that I will revive and complete the Ajaokuta steel mill. item.title: Liam Delap’s struggles are symbolic of damaging Chelsea churn
item.description: The constant turnover of players and staff has made consistency an elusive quality at Stamford Bridge Liam Delap came and went. He joined Chelsea in the summer of 2025 and was hailed by Enzo Maresca as the next Harry Kane. Fast forward a year, though, and there was no chance of Delap joining Kane in England’s World Cup squad. The striker’s form was miserable and the only surprise was that Chelsea made a profit when they sold him to Nottingham Forest for £50m last summer. On one level it looks like good business. Delap’s only season at Stamford Bridge featured one serious hamstring injury, one league goal, one ridiculous red card and not much else. Analysts at other clubs rated him at Ipswich and felt Chelsea was the wrong fit for his direct style of play. The mistake was less the decision not to give Delap another season, no matter the worries over cover for João Pedro, more the call to sign him in the first place. Continue reading...
item.dc:creator: Jacob Steinberg
item.content:encoded: The constant turnover of players and staff has made consistency an elusive quality at Stamford Bridge Liam Delap came and went. He joined Chelsea in the summer of 2025 and was hailed by Enzo Maresca as the next Harry Kane. Fast forward a year, though, and there was no chance of Delap joining Kane in England’s World Cup squad. The striker’s form was miserable and the only surprise was that Chelsea made a profit when they sold him to Nottingham Forest for £50m last summer. On one level it looks like good business. Delap’s only season at Stamford Bridge featured one serious hamstring injury, one league goal, one ridiculous red card and not much else. Analysts at other clubs rated him at Ipswich and felt Chelsea was the wrong fit for his direct style of play. The mistake was less the decision not to give Delap another season, no matter the worries over cover for João Pedro, more the call to sign him in the first place. Continue reading...

item.title: Volvo's big batteries: We drive its updated 2028 plug-in hybrids
item.description: Volvo provided flights from Washington, DC, to Copenhagen, Denmark, and accommodation so Ars could drive the XC60 and XC90 plug-in hybrids. Ars does not accept paid editorial content. COPENHAGEN, Denmark—If we lived in the world that Volvo’s product planners expected back when the current XC90 debuted in 2015 , both it and the smaller but related XC60 (which arrived in 2017) might have been the last of their kind as everything went electric . As we know, the future hasn’t turned out quite like that, especially in the critically important US market . At the same time, Europe and China are electrifying, which seems like an argument against spending resources on developing all-new replacements for models that might not have an eight-year lifespan in most markets. So instead, Volvo has given the XC60 and XC90 another lifecycle refresh. The exterior styling tweaks are minimal; the bigger three-row XC90 had already been given a new look last year, and the XC60 now gains a similar grille and the same matrix headlights, for instance. And that’s no bad thing—both were, and remain, handsome shapes that are popular with Volvo’s customer base. Instead, the Swedish automaker’s attention has been on bringing the technology up to date for model year 2028 standards. Which means a much bigger battery for the PHEVs, with sufficient capacity for a couple of days of daily driving for most of us before needing to be recharged. There’s also new, modern infotainment and interiors that are now even nicer to spend time in than before. Read full article Comments

item.title: Support team put in an emergency order for vodka – lots of vodka – to bring PCs back online
item.description: The end of the working week is often enough to drive tech support people to drink, which is why The Register likes to get the party started early. Friday mornings bring a new installment of On Call – the column in which we share your stories of doing whatever it takes to keep tech running. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Bruce," who told us that in the mid-2000s he worked for a global radio station. "We used to have about 30 PCs, all running slightly different radio shows depending on the time zone where we broadcast," he explained. The PCs were old clunkers running Windows 95 long after Microsoft ended support for the OS. Management knew the machines needed replacing, but funding was probably another year away. "We had to coax them on till then," Bruce wrote. "And by coax, I mean we were buying RAM on eBay because nobody sold the 4MB sticks we needed anymore." Thanks to the tender ministrations of Bruce and his colleagues, the PCs kept humming and the radio stations stayed on the air. Until a lovely spring Tuesday, when Bruce and his crew enjoyed a bucolic cup of tea in the first real sunshine of the season and received a call informing them that one of the stations was down. One of Bruce's mates figured a cranky old PC probably just needed a reboot and headed off to fix it while the rest of the team enjoyed their tea. And then the phone rang again to report another outage, so Bruce and the entire crew went back to work, chatting about which switch or other shared device could have taken out two PCs. When they arrived in the office, the chap who had gone to reboot the first PC ran in and announced that the computer room had flooded. Bruce and his teammates ran into that room and found dirty brown water all over the floor, walls, ceiling, and the racks holding the ancient PCs. "Water was even spraying out of the front fans of the last two PCs that were still working," Bruce told The Register . "After a lot of shouting words unfit to print, we all got to work ripping them out, shutting down what we could that looked to be working, and started lining them up outside in the car park," Bruce wrote. "Some of us then got to work stripping them down into component parts, others washed them down with isopropanol." As the isopropanol supply dwindled, one of the team arranged an urgent delivery of vodka. "Luckily, it was a gloriously sunny day, so we quickly rinsed the PCs and left them to dry, strewn all over the car park," Bruce wrote. By this stage, he and the team were all filthy and exhausted. With the stations still offline, they had to rebuild the PCs and get them running again. "We only lost two sticks of RAM, one sound card, and a power supply," Bruce wrote. The culprit turned out to be a new hire on the facilities team who, while touring the building, had turned a random tap to see what would happen. "It released water from a stagnant iron tank that sat there rusting away for years," Bruce wrote. For reasons nobody understood, the tan

item.content:encoded: The end of the working week is often enough to drive tech support people to drink, which is why The Register likes to get the party started early. Friday mornings bring a new installment of On Call – the column in which we share your stories of doing whatever it takes to keep tech running. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Bruce," who told us that in the mid-2000s he worked for a global radio station. "We had to coax them on till then," Bruce wrote. "And by coax, I mean we were buying RAM on eBay because nobody sold the 4MB sticks we needed anymore." Thanks to the tender ministrations of Bruce and his colleagues, the PCs kept humming and the radio stations stayed on the air. Until a lovely spring Tuesday, when Bruce and his crew enjoyed a bucolic cup of tea in the first real sunshine of the season and received a call informing them that one of the stations was down. One of Bruce's mates figured a cranky old PC probably just needed a reboot and headed off to fix it while the rest of the team enjoyed their tea. And then the phone rang again to report another outage, so Bruce and the entire crew went back to work, chatting about which switch or other shared device could have taken out two PCs. When they arrived in the office, the chap who had gone to reboot the first PC ran in and announced that the computer room had flooded. Bruce and his teammates ran into that room and found dirty brown water all over the floor, walls, ceiling, and the racks holding the ancient PCs. "Water was even spraying out of the front fans of the last two PCs that were still working," Bruce told The Register . "After a lot of shouting words unfit to print, we all got to work ripping them out, shutting down what we could that looked to be working, and started lining them up outside in the car park," Bruce wrote. "Some of us then got to work stripping them down into component parts, others washed them down with isopropanol." As the isopropanol supply dwindled, one of the team arranged an urgent delivery of vodka. "Luckily, it was a gloriously sunny day, so we quickly rinsed the PCs and left them to dry, strewn all over the car park," Bruce wrote. By this stage, he and the team were all filthy and exhausted. With the stations still offline, they had to rebuild the PCs and get them running again. "We only lost two sticks of RAM, one sound card, and a power supply," Bruce wrote. The culprit turned out to be a new hire on the facilities team who, while touring the building, had turned a random tap to see what would happen. "It released water from a stagnant iron tank that sat there rusting away for years," Bruce wrote. For reasons nobody understood, the tank drained through a pipe into the room housing the broadcast PCs. Have you had to clean up hardware in a hurry, perhaps with odd substances or implements? If so, click here to send On Call your story. We'll raise a glass to each one of you who sends a story and do it again if we share it on a future Friday. ®

item.title: Natural England objected to a datacentre. Weeks later ministers threatened to abolish the agency
item.description: Body urged Bristol city council to reject plan because of risk to nearby protected wildlife and habitats Natural England objected to the building of a large AI datacentre near Bristol weeks before the government threatened to abolish the independent environmental adviser. The nature adviser made a significant intervention to urge Bristol city council not to grant planning permission for a 40MW datacentre at Avonmouth, because of the threat to protected wildlife and habitats at one of the UK’s most important sites for migratory birds, which is within 600 metres of the site.
