item.title: Weird 'potato chips' and 'ghostly rocks' on Mars spotted by NASA rovers Curiosity and Perseverance
item.description: null NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance rovers have spotted a bizarre assortment of Martian oddities, from potato chip-like rocks and ghostly white formations to mysterious patterns etched into the Red Planet's surface. While their appearances may be unusual, these formations offer scientists something far more valuable than a collection of curious snapshots: clues to the geological processes that shaped Mars over billions of years. In particular, the rocks and mineral deposits could help researchers piece together the planet's watery past and identify environments that may once have been capable of supporting microbial life. NASA's Curiosity rover recently wrapped up a drilling campaign at a location nicknamed "Nazca," where scientists have been examining unusual disk-shaped crystal formations embedded in the surrounding bedrock. Some of the features are so thin and flat that the mission team likened them to potato chips, according to a statement from the space agency. NASA's Curiosity rover captured a close-up view of unusual, disk-shaped crystal formations embedded in Martian bedrock using its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI) on Nov. 7, 2026 (Sol 5067). The thin, flattened formations resemble tiny potato chips. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS) Curiosity used its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI), mounted on the end of its robotic arm, to capture detailed close-up images of the formations on Nov. 7 — the rover's 5,067th Martian day , or Sol 5067. The rover also used its ChemCam instrument to study the rocks' chemical composition, while samples from the Nazca drill site were delivered to its onboard Sample Analysis at Mars (SAM) instrument for further analysis. Meanwhile, NASA's Perseverance rover has been investigating a collection of unusually bright rocks in an area called "Idubi," located in the “Lac de Charmes” region outside Jezero Crater. The rover captured images of the formations on Oct. 29, 2026 (Sol 2023), revealing pale, ghostly-looking rocks that stand out dramatically against the darker, dust-covered Martian landscape. Data from Perseverance's SuperCam instrument revealed that the rocks are rich in hydrated silica rather than being typical igneous rocks. That discovery has scientists particularly interested. On Earth, hydrated silica can form in environments involving hydrothermal activity or groundwater. These deposits are also capable of preserving microscopic fossils, making them valuable targets in the search for evidence of ancient life, according to another statement from NASA. NASA's Perseverance rover captured unusually bright, silica-rich rock in the "Idubi" area outside Jezero Crater on Oct. 29, 2026 (Sol 2023), using its left Mastcam-Z camera. The pale formation stands out against the darker, dust-covered Martian terrain. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/ASU) Perseverance is now conducting a closer investigation of the formations, using its instruments to gather detailed chemical and mineralogical data that could help scient

item.content:encoded: null NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance rovers have spotted a bizarre assortment of Martian oddities, from potato chip-like rocks and ghostly white formations to mysterious patterns etched into the Red Planet's surface. Some of the features are so thin and flat that the mission team likened them to potato chips, according to a statement from the space agency. NASA's Curiosity rover captured a close-up view of unusual, disk-shaped crystal formations embedded in Martian bedrock using its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI) on Nov. 7, 2026 (Sol 5067). The thin, flattened formations resemble tiny potato chips. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS) Curiosity used its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI), mounted on the end of its robotic arm, to capture detailed close-up images of the formations on Nov. 7 — the rover's 5,067th Martian day , or Sol 5067. The rover also used its ChemCam instrument to study the rocks' chemical composition, while samples from the Nazca drill site were delivered to its onboard Sample Analysis at Mars (SAM) instrument for further analysis. Meanwhile, NASA's Perseverance rover has been investigating a collection of unusually bright rocks in an area called "Idubi," located in the “Lac de Charmes” region outside Jezero Crater. The rover captured images of the formations on Oct. 29, 2026 (Sol 2023), revealing pale, ghostly-looking rocks that stand out dramatically against the darker, dust-covered Martian landscape. Data from Perseverance's SuperCam instrument revealed that the rocks are rich in hydrated silica rather than being typical igneous rocks. That discovery has scientists particularly interested. On Earth, hydrated silica can form in environments involving hydrothermal activity or groundwater. These deposits are also capable of preserving microscopic fossils, making them valuable targets in the search for evidence of ancient life, according to another statement from NASA. NASA's Perseverance rover captured unusually bright, silica-rich rock in the "Idubi" area outside Jezero Crater on Oct. 29, 2026 (Sol 2023), using its left Mastcam-Z camera. The pale formation stands out against the darker, dust-covered Martian terrain. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/ASU) Perseverance is now conducting a closer investigation of the formations, using its instruments to gather detailed chemical and mineralogical data that could help scientists determine how the rocks formed and whether they preserve potential signs of past microbial activity. NASA's Curiosity rover captured this view of distinctive polygon-shaped patterns outlined by raised ridges in the Martian bedrock using its Mast Camera (Mastcam) on Nov. 13, 2026 (Sol 5073). The unusual textures resemble formations the rover encountered earlier in its climb up Mount Sharp. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS) Back at Mount Sharp , Curiosity has also spotted another geological curiosity: the return of distinctive polygon-shaped patterns across the Martian bedrock. The rover's latest images, captured on Nov. 13, 2026 (Sol 5073), show small, regularly shaped polygons outlined by raised ridges, resembling patterns the rover encountered earlier in its climb up the layered mountain, whose rocky slopes preserve a record of Mars' changing climate and ancient watery environments. Scientists say these formations could have developed through several processes, including mineral shrinkage as water evaporated, temperature changes or the expansion and compaction of buried sediments, according to a statement from NASA. By studying the composition of the rocks and the material cementing the raised ridges around the polygons , researchers hope to determine which processes shaped the terrain. Together, these discoveries highlight how much Mars' seemingly barren landscape can reveal about its past. As Curiosity continues climbing Mount Sharp and Perseverance investigates ancient terrain beyond Jezero Crater , both rovers are helping piece together the planet's unique features and complex geological history.

item.title: Mauricio Pochettino can now see just how desperate Manchester United are | Jonathan Wilson
item.description: The manager’s first game in charge was a disaster and he needs to lift the mood within a sunken squad if a relegation battle is to be avoided Sign up for our free newsletter here In as much as any derby can ever be a free hit, there was always a sense that Mauricio Pochettino’s first game as Manchester United manager wouldn’t matter too much; nobody expected them to win away to Liverpool. This was not a game on which anybody was going to judge him, and that feeling only magnified when Leny Yoro was sent off after eight minutes. United’s victory at Anfield last season was their first for a decade; what’s difficult to do with 11 men is only going to get harder playing a man down for 82 minutes. But that does not mean that it did not matter. Although Roy Keane was determined to reject the suggestion, there was perhaps even some credit to be gleaned from having lost only 4-0 . Certainly when they were 2-0 down after 13 minutes, there was reason for United to fear an embarrassment akin to their 7-0 defeat against Liverpool in 2023 . Perhaps Pochettino deserves credit for his switch to a back three, which brought a degree of stabilisation, but United could easily have lost far more comfortably than they did. Liverpool had 18 shots in the game three-and-a-half years ago, eight of them on target; on Sunday they had 28, 11 of them on target. When you’ve conceded an xG of 4.38, there’s not much point quibbling over the details; you’ve been hammered. Continue reading...
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Wilson
item.content:encoded: The manager’s first game in charge was a disaster and he needs to lift the mood within a sunken squad if a relegation battle is to be avoided Sign up for our free newsletter here In as much as any derby can ever be a free hit, there was always a sense that Mauricio Pochettino’s first game as Manchester United manager wouldn’t matter too much; nobody expected them to win away to Liverpool. This was not a game on which anybody was going to judge him, and that feeling only magnified when Leny Yoro was sent off after eight minutes. United’s victory at Anfield last season was their first for a decade; what’s difficult to do with 11 men is only going to get harder playing a man down for 82 minutes. But that does not mean that it did not matter. Although Roy Keane was determined to reject the suggestion, there was perhaps even some credit to be gleaned from having lost only 4-0 . Certainly when they were 2-0 down after 13 minutes, there was reason for United to fear an embarrassment akin to their 7-0 defeat against Liverpool in 2023 . Perhaps Pochettino deserves credit for his switch to a back three, which brought a degree of stabilisation, but United could easily have lost far more comfortably than they did. Liverpool had 18 shots in the game three-and-a-half years ago, eight of them on target; on Sunday they had 28, 11 of them on target. When you’ve conceded an xG of 4.38, there’s not much point quibbling over the details; you’ve been hammered. Continue reading...

item.title: 'Avengers: Doomsday' gets final trailer, explaining why Steve Rogers is back and showing an epic battle with the X-Men
item.description: The final trailer for Avengers: Doomsday just landed, and it finally puts the spotlight on our boy Steve Rogers. Avengers: Doomsday has been promising the scale and excitement the MCU has often been lacking since the Infinity Saga. Previous trailers played it safe, mostly setting up the conflict and introducing Victor Von Doom. Now it’s time for one last explosive look at the film before it tries to conquer cinemas next month. Disney and Marvel Studios have just released a "final trailer" that puts the focus back on Steve Rogers — no longer Captain America but still ready to use Mjolnir — and Thor as the veterans leading the New Avengers, former colleagues, the Fantastic Four, and even Fox's X-Men (after some first-encounter fights, of course) against Doom and his followers. A few dodgy CG shots aside, it looks grand, and if you're a big X-Men fan, it's hard not to get goosebumps when Cyclops (James Marsden) finally gets to say the thing. The multiverse-spanning story is still largely kept a secret in this trailer, but at least we get a better sense of what the emotional stakes are for Rogers and how all these heroes can realistically work together against the greatest threat they've faced so far (even if most of them won't get more than a few lines). (Image credit: Marvel) As for Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom, this isn't his trailer, but the mysterious Latverian witches — who have fueled many theories online for months — are finally seen in motion. Doom has, however, received a simple but evocative poster that mirrors one of the original Iron Man ones. Even though Marvel Studios' honcho, Kevin Feige, has shot down the theory that this Victor Von Doom is a Tony Stark variant , you can't stop marketing from doing the obvious things, it seems. We won't complain. (Image credit: Marvel Studios) Avengers: Doomsday won't fix all of the Multiverse Saga's shortcomings, but at the very least, it looks like a proper fun time with more toys being mashed together than ever before and proper stakes. Right before Christmas, it's hard to resist such a pitch. Avengers: Doomsday assembles on December 18, 2026, only in cinemas...Yes, it opens the same day as Dune: Part Three . item.title: The remains of a long-dead volcano on Mars | Space photo of the day for Nov. 23, 2026
item.description: null An image of Tharsis Tholus, a volcano on the surface of Mars, produced by ESA's Mars Express orbiter. (Image credit: ESA/DLR/FU Berlin) Researchers have spotted an ancient, "dead" Martian volcano from orbit around the Red Planet. What is it? The European Space Agency's Mars Express spacecraft, which has been orbiting and studying the planet since it arrived in 2003, recently captured incredible new imagery of the volcano Tharsis Tholus. This snapshot was captured by the spacecraft's High Resolution Stereo Camera. Even as old and worn as it is, the Martian volcano stands at around 4.97 miles (8 kilometers) tall which is comparable to some of the highest peaks in the Himalayan mountains. Despite its impressive height, it's still only about a medium-sized volcano for Mars, which is home much more impressively-sized volcanoes. For example, the planet's largest volcano Olympus Mons measures in at roughly 13.2 miles high (21.3 kilometers). Tharsis Tholus, a volcano on the surface of Mars, as seen by ESA's Mars Express orbiter. (Image credit: ESA/DLR/FU Berlin) Why is it incredible? While Tharsis Tholus might not be the tallest volcano on Mars, it is incredibly steep. It is steeper than Mauna Kea in Hawaii on Earth. To fully showcase the volcano's structure and topography in 3D, researchers actually exaggerated the vertical scale in this image, ESA reported . In addition to being steep and fairly tall, the volcano also has an interesting history. You can see that it is speckled with what look like small holes which are actually craters created by impacts from objects like asteroids. The volcano's current, unique shape is a combined effort by these impacts, environmental factors causing erosion and warping and ancient lava flows that left behind built-up material. The observations by Mars Express also reveals cracks and other imperfections in the volcano. All of these details might seem like superficial bits of detail, however every small crater, every lumpy cliffside and every worn down surface hides information about the planet's past. By studying features like volcanoes on Mars, researchers can piece together what the planet may have looked like in its ancient past. How active was this volcano? How did it interact with the landscape around it? Observations like this can hold the answers.

item.title: Ghana’s Black Challenge Conquer the World With First-Ever Amputee Football World Cup Title
item.description: Pure joy on the pitch as Ghana’s Black Challenge mark their historic 2026 WAFF Amputee Football World Cup triumph in Mexico. Ghana’s national amputee football team, the Black Challenge, have officially conquered the world after edging Morocco 1–0 in the final of the 2026 World Amputee Football Federation (WAFF) World Cup in San Juan de los Lagos, Mexico on Sunday, November 22, 2026. For anyone keeping an eye on international football and West African sporting milestones, this is a moment worth celebrating—it marks Ghana’s very first Amputee Football World Cup crown. The championship match brought together two African powerhouses and served as a high-stakes showdown between familiar rivals, following Ghana’s earlier continental triumphs against Morocco, including the 2024 African Amputee Cup of Nations final. Captain Richard Arthur Opentil stepped up as the decisive hero, scoring the lone goal in the 32nd minute. From there, Ghana dug deep with grit, smart positioning, and defensive discipline to shut out Morocco and bring the trophy home. Intense action between Morocco and Ghana during the 2026 WAFF Amputee Football World Cup in Mexico. What makes Ghana’s run in Mexico even more memorable is how much they had to overcome in the knockout stages. The Black Challenge defeated the United States 3–1 in the Round of 16, eased past Egypt 2–0 in the quarter-finals behind a brace from forward Mubarik Mohammed , and then edged a tense semi-final 1–1 after extra time before winning 4–3 on penalties. Individual brilliance shone right alongside the team trophy. Forward Mubarik Mohammed finished as the tournament’s top scorer with seven goals, earning the Golden Boot award. Back home, the achievement sparked widespread celebration, with congratulatory messages from Ghana’s leadership—including President John Dramani Mahama and the Ministry of Sports and Recreation—alongside financial backing and pledges from corporate supporters and philanthropists such as Gold Fields Ghana and Mohammed Raii through the EEZZY Group Foundation. Speaking after the victory, captain Richard Arthur Opentil dedicated the triumph to Ghana and its supporters as an early Christmas gift to the nation. Ghana’s Black Challenge celebrate lifting their maiden 2026 WAFF Amputee Football World Cup trophy in San Juan de los Lagos, Mexico. If you are wondering what the WAFF Amputee Football World Cup is all about, it is the premier international championship for amputee football, governed globally by the World Amputee Football Federation (WAFF). Played according to rules adapted from FIFA’s Laws of the Game, amputee football is fast-paced, physically demanding, and thrilling to watch. Matches feature seven players per side—outfield players with lower-limb amputations playing on forearm crutches without prostheses, and goalkeepers with single-arm amputations—with crutches treated as part of the player’s body rather than a tool to intentionally play the ball. Goalkeeper Razak and the Black Challe

item.title: Esposito emulates Vieri with Inter hat-trick but De Ketelaere haunts him again
item.description: Italy’s new cover star enjoyed a ‘beautiful’ treble but could not celebrate it after his side threw away two-goal leads three times to draw 4-4 with Atalanta This ought to have been a magic moment for Pio Esposito. He had just scored his first Serie A hat-trick, becoming only the third Italian to get one for Inter in the era of three points for a win. The last to do it was Christian Vieri, back in 2003. Two years before Esposito was born. We will come back to that. Esposito has been drawing premature comparisons to Vieri for some time and especially now after a barnstorming November in which he has scored eight times in five games, including three in two for his country, and two of those as part of a man-of-the-match performance during an upset win against France . item.title: I’m planning my first dark sky trip, and all because this educational star projector showed me what I’m missing
item.description: I didn’t expect much as I unboxed the Brainstorm Night Sky; after all, I’m significantly older than this educational star projector’s target audience. Perhaps I’d come away with a sense of wonder and delight, coupled with mild irritation at having to hunt down three AA batteries to power it. Instead, I was filled with envy as the Brainstorm Night Sky reminded me just what I was missing, thanks to the rigors of light pollution . A few minutes after powering it down, I was already making plans for my first dark sky trip, yearning for a view that rivaled the Brainstorm’s cosmic images. Brainstorm Night Sky Projector review Whatever your age, the Brainstorm Night Sky is so simple to use The Brainstorm Night Sky projector comes with four or six slides, depending on whether you buy the blue or gray version (Image credit: Chris McMullen) Draw the curtains, press the Night Sky’s single button (tilting the projector and twisting the focus as appropriate) and it projects a circular image onto a ceiling or wall. Press the button again and the projection slowly begins to rotate, slowly but stutter-free. It really is that simple to operate and, aimed at budding astronomers aged eight or above, it's reasonably lightweight without feeling flimsy. Depending on the model you buy, you’ll get four or six interchangeable slides. (Image credit: Chris McMullen) Specifications Weight: 14.8 oz (420 g) Bulb type: Non-specified Laser: No Control: On-unit Rotation: Yes, one speed Projection area: Up to 8.2 ft (2.5 m) Sleep timer: Yes (30 mins) Power: 3x AA batteries Speaker: No I was initially a little surprised by the size of the projection: at up to 8.2 feet (2.5 m) wide it’s not going to fill an entire ceiling. It also switches off after 30 minutes, a limit that can’t be disabled, so if you’re looking to put on your own space-themed party this is not the projector for you. But it’s on point for home education and, priced from $49.99, the Brainstorm Night Sky projector won’t break the bank. There’s minimal distortion around the edge of the images; the planets are spherical from the word go, unlike some projectors where I’ve had to tweak them to stop Mars turning into an egg. And I never once had to crane my neck because half the solar system had been projected onto a bookcase. This projector revealed what light pollution had taken from me There are two slides featuring the Northern Hemisphere’s starscape, with and without labelled constellations. item.dc:creator: Chris McMullen
item.content:encoded: I didn’t expect much as I unboxed the Brainstorm Night Sky; after all, I’m significantly older than this educational star projector’s target audience. Perhaps I’d come away with a sense of wonder and delight, coupled with mild irritation at having to hunt down three AA batteries to power it. Press the button again and the projection slowly begins to rotate, slowly but stutter-free. It really is that simple to operate and, aimed at budding astronomers aged eight or above, it's reasonably lightweight without feeling flimsy. Depending on the model you buy, you’ll get four or six interchangeable slides. (Image credit: Chris McMullen) Specifications Weight: 14.8 oz (420 g) Bulb type: Non-specified Laser: No Control: On-unit Rotation: Yes, one speed Projection area: Up to 8.2 ft (2.5 m) Sleep timer: Yes (30 mins) Power: 3x AA batteries Speaker: No I was initially a little surprised by the size of the projection: at up to 8.2 feet (2.5 m) wide it’s not going to fill an entire ceiling. It also switches off after 30 minutes, a limit that can’t be disabled, so if you’re looking to put on your own space-themed party this is not the projector for you. But it’s on point for home education and, priced from $49.99, the Brainstorm Night Sky projector won’t break the bank. There’s minimal distortion around the edge of the images; the planets are spherical from the word go, unlike some projectors where I’ve had to tweak them to stop Mars turning into an egg. And I never once had to crane my neck because half the solar system had been projected onto a bookcase. This projector revealed what light pollution had taken from me There are two slides featuring the Northern Hemisphere’s starscape, with and without labelled constellations. Chris McMullen There are two slides featuring the Northern Hemisphere’s starscape, with and without labelled constellations. Chris McMullen There are two slides featuring the Northern Hemisphere’s starscape, with and without labelled constellations. Chris McMullen The Brainstorm Night Sky model I tested comes with four slides, each with a case to protect them from smudges and sticky fingers. You place one into the provided slide housing then insert that into the projector. There’s the moon, the solar system, and two showing the Northern Hemisphere’s night sky, as seen from Hawaii (a key location for astronomy). I can appreciate the educational value of the first couple, even if I am still seething at Pluto being demoted back in 2006. But it was the latter pair of slides that really opened my eyes to what I could be seeing over my head. I can spot maybe 10-20 stars from my backyard, cloud cover permitting; thanks to light pollution , that’s it. Even though the best stargazing apps can show me what I should see, when I step outside, all I typically see with the naked eye is the odd pinprick in the void. The Brainstorm Night Sky uses three AA batteries, but they’re not included with the projector. (Image credit: Chris McMullen) But as soon as I inserted that third slide, a striking stellar display appeared above my head, with more stars than I could hope to count. Even knowing that Hawaii’s night sky stretches far further than eight feet across, the difference between this view and the one from my house was like night and day. Brainstorm claims this slide features over 20,000 stars, though that’s likely referring to the source photo rather than the projected image. The fourth slide — the same crisp starscape but with every visible constellation labelled — was almost as attention-grabbing. Educational value aside, it drove home that I couldn’t see the majority of these star patterns to name them, my local night sky is that polluted. Knowing what I was missing out on made me determined to take my stargazing further afield. Some of the best smart telescopes can lessen the impact of light pollution, but stepping away from skyglow is the most effective option. Hawaii’s a little far to travel, but I’ve already started looking into local dark sky sites. I just need to grab a pair of the best binoculars for stargazing , hop on my bike and I’m ready to go. The Brainstorm Night Sky is a solid, budget-priced educational tool, but it has one drawback You can purchase one additional Southern Hemisphere slide, but beyond that you’re limited to the included slides. (Image credit: Chris McMullen) The Brainstorm Night Sky’s projections are crisp enough that you can easily make out every constellation name, but they could be a hair brighter. The Ainael Meter Galaxy Projector , for example, delivers more illumination. If you want to use the Brainstorm Night Sky to relax, the rotate function gives its projections an oddly hypnotic effect, and the device is whisper-quiet to boot. And while Brainstorm doesn’t specify battery life, one set of rechargeables lasted me for several days. Unfortunately, the Brainstorm Night Sky's slide collection is a little limited. There are two models, a blue version with four slides (the one I tested) and a gray version with six slides (featuring additional space shuttle and black hole images). The included instructions state you can purchase an additional slide disc showing the Southern Hemisphere’s stars, but that’s a maximum of seven images. Nor is this projector compatible with the slides from the Brainstorm Deep Sky Projector It’s a little disappointing given that Brainstorm has clearly put thought into the projector’s educational value. Those instructions double as a poster of the solar system, and children can use a “secret code” (printed on the instructions) to explore more astronomy facts on the company’s website. Offering extra slide packs, of the kind you can buy for the Pococo Galaxy Projector , would give it more long-term appeal. As is, I can see its novelty and educational value diminishing over time, at which point you can upgrade to one of the best star projectors . If you’re not bothered by the lack of expandability, the Brainstorm Night Sky’s price, image quality and ease of use still make it a useful tool for kindling a child’s interest in astronomy, or as a budget-friendly gift for junior stargazers. It’s certainly spurred me into action — how much is a plane ticket to Hawaii, anyway?

item.title: What did the Soviet Union's final deep space probe actually see on Mars?
item.description:
Micah Hanks is a science reporter and podcaster focusing on space and astronomy, and Editor at TheDebrief.org. Follow him on X @MicahHanks.

On July 12, 1988, Phobos 2 — one of the Soviet Union's final major planetary exploration probes — was launched from Baikonur Cosmodrome aboard a Proton rocket. The spacecraft's mission included the study of Mars and the Martian moon Phobos, with a planned close approach and deployment of landing probes, and over the next several months, the spacecraft successfully captured more than three dozen images of Phobos during its time in service. However, early in the following year, the spacecraft's mission abruptly ended after the Phobos 2 ground team mysteriously lost contact with the spacecraft. Adding to the mystery were objects in some of the final photographs dispatched by the doomed spacecraft, which seemed to show an elongated shadow beneath the probe — a strange twist in one of the Soviet Union's final space missions, and one that soon gave rise to conspiracy theories about what the fate of Phobos 2 might have been. So what caused the odd-looking appearance of the shadow in the final images captured by Phobos 2, and what was the real reason behind the spacecraft's sudden failure? Last of the Soviet space explorers Originally, the Soviet Union had planned for Phobos 2 to reach the Red Planet by late January 1989, after which the spacecraft would begin collecting data about the Martian environment leading up to its initial contact with Mars' largest moon in early June. item.content:encoded:
Micah Hanks is a science reporter and podcaster focusing on space and astronomy, and Editor at TheDebrief.org. Follow him on X @MicahHanks.

On July 12, 1988, Phobos 2 — one of the Soviet Union's final major planetary exploration probes — was launched from Baikonur Cosmodrome aboard a Proton rocket. The spacecraft's mission included the study of Mars and the Martian moon Phobos, with a planned close approach and deployment of landing probes, and over the next several months, the spacecraft successfully captured more than three dozen images of Phobos during its time in service. However, early in the following year, the spacecraft's mission abruptly ended after the Phobos 2 ground team mysteriously lost contact with the spacecraft. Adding to the mystery were objects in some of the final photographs dispatched by the doomed spacecraft, which seemed to show an elongated shadow beneath the probe — a strange twist in one of the Soviet Union's final space missions, and one that soon gave rise to conspiracy theories about what the fate of Phobos 2 might have been. So what caused the odd-looking appearance of the shadow in the final images captured by Phobos 2, and what was the real reason behind the spacecraft's sudden failure? Last of the Soviet space explorers Originally, the Soviet Union had planned for Phobos 2 to reach the Red Planet by late January 1989, after which the spacecraft would begin collecting data about the Martian environment leading up to its initial contact with Mars' largest moon in early June. A model of one of the Phobos spacecraft on display in the Memorial Museum of Cosmonautics in Moscow, Russia. (Image credit: Музей Космонавтики from Россия, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons) To say that a lot hinged on the success of the mission would be an understatement, given the unfortunate fate of the probe's predecessor, Phobos 1, which went offline on Sept. 2, 1988, after a faulty command sequence was initiated while the spacecraft was on its way to Mars. The stakes were almost immediately raised as Phobos 2 arrived in orbit around Mars on Jan. 30, 1989 , when one of the probe's three onboard flight system processors was found to have gone offline, with another already experiencing technical issues. Over the course of the next several weeks, Phobos 2 was able to overcome some of these setbacks and successfully began sending useful scientific data about the Martian environment back to Earth. By March, all the probe's science instruments appeared to be functioning normally, and despite the earlier loss of one of its processors, the remaining two had continued to facilitate control of the spacecraft by its Soviet ground control team. An image of Phobos captured by the Soviet Union's Phobos 2 probe. (Image credit: Roscosmos) Unexplained failure That all changed on March 27, 1989, as Phobos 2 prepared to capture navigational images of its namesake as the Martian moon passed, which would be useful in advance of another forthcoming flyby in early April. Achieving this meant that the probe had to be angled in such a way that it faced Phobos, whereby its communications antennas would be temporarily directed away from Earth. During the imaging portion of the maneuver, all appeared to go smoothly, but soon afterward, ground controllers realized they were unable to reestablish contact with the probe. An image of Mars and its moon Phobos captured by the Soviet Union's Phobos 2 spacecraft on Feb. 28, 1989. Phobos 2 took a total of 13 color sets of images of Phobos before contact was lost on March 27, 1989. (Image credit: Roscosmos) A few fleeting radio contacts were made over the ensuing hours, which engineers believed might indicate that during the period of signal loss required for imagery of Phobos to be obtained, the spacecraft may have begun to spin uncontrollably. If this were the case, and the spacecraft could not reorient its solar panels toward the sun, it would eventually lose all power. No further contact with Phobos 2 could be established beyond this point, although images from the probe's final close encounter with the Martian moon were successfully delivered back to Soviet ground controllers. While investigators identified a failure involving the spacecraft's onboard computer system as the most probable explanation, to this day, the exact cause of the events leading to the loss remains unknown. Theories involving the failure Although questions remain about the fate of Phobos 2, several theories have been put forward over the years. According to authors Paolo Ulivi and David M. Harland , one of the simplest explanations was that the spacecraft was damaged after an impact with other material orbiting the Martian moon, although later modeling by Soviet engineers and American teams at NASA's Jet Propulsion Lab seemed to rule this out. The final image transmitted from the Soviet Union's Phobos 2 spacecraft shortly before losing communication with Earth. (Image credit: Roscosmos) A more likely scenario involved failure of the probe's second attitude control computer, which had already begun experiencing technical issues as Phobos 2 arrived in Martian orbit. With two of its three processors now offline, the third and sole remaining computer was unable to maintain control of the spacecraft on its own. An additional factor might have been power loss from battery drainage while the probe's solar arrays were directed away from the sun, and with no failsafe to power down any non-critical systems under such conditions, the spacecraft would likely have undergone significant power loss. However, the probe's failure was only one part of the mystery: equally perplexing had been the unusual images Phobos 2 captured in its final moments, which later sparked speculation — and conspiracy theories — about what might have been behind the spacecraft's sudden demise. The shadow in Phobos 2's final photos Soviet test pilot Marina Popovich. (Image credit: Keystone/Hulton Archive/Getty Images) In some of the final images captured by Phobos 2, an unusual, elongated shadow had been visible in the frame, which with time would begin to prompt the most unusual of all the theories about the probe's demise: that it had been disabled by an alien spacecraft. Among the proponents of this theory had been Marina Popovich, a former experimental pilot and the first Soviet woman to break the sound barrier, who set over 100 world aviation records in her career. In 1991, Popovich held a press conference at the Soviet Consulate in San Francisco, where she claimed a cigar-shaped object had been photographed near the Martian moon, which she believed to be an alien mothership . Given her storied background in Soviet aerospace history, Popovich's views likely carried a degree of credibility unlike most others. However, that did not make them accurate. Explaining the Phobos "shadow" Determining what the images actually show requires an understanding of the probe's orbit, particularly with relation to the Martian moon it was attempting to photograph. At the time, the spacecraft and Phobos were in almost the same orbit, and moving at very similar speeds. As Ulivi and Harland note , due to these conditions, the probe's Termoskan multispectral imager often captured images that "included the shadow of the moon on the planet's surface as a dark oblong cigar-shaped feature." In 1991, a NASA-led study of the Termoskan observations concluded that the unusual appearance of the shadow most likely resulted from a combination of factors acting together. The study team attributed these to the scanning instrument itself, as well as the spacecraft's near-co-orbital motion with Phobos, its viewing direction, and finally, a slight rocking motion the researchers concluded the spacecraft had likely exhibited at the time. item.title: Astronomers just discovered a rare triple star system 28 light-years away, and they have ‘no clean explanation for how it got here’
item.description: A triple system containing a dim red dwarf star and not one but two white dwarfs has been fortuitously discovered just 28 light-years away from our solar system. "We were actually looking for planets ," Étienne Artigau of the Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets at the Université de Montréal, who led the discovery, said in a statement . "Instead, we found something much more surprising." So surprising that there are no similar systems within at least 100 light-years . Furthermore, the configuration of the system seems impossible. "This system should not exist," added Montreal's Patrick Dufour. "We have no clean explanation for how it got here." This triple system has been called Welopō'ai, which is a portmanteau of two Hawaiian words that means a 'path of family traits', and to understand the mystery behind it requires astronomers to figure out the history of the three objects. A white dwarf is what remains when a star of similar mass to our sun reaches the end of its life. As it begins to run low on hydrogen for nuclear fusion reactions in its core, the star's energy generation begins to falter and its interior starts to contract under gravity . This has the effect of raising the temperature throughout the star, causing an outer shell of hydrogen to ignite its own fusion reactions. The star promptly bloats to become a red giant tens or even hundreds of millions of kilometers across. Soon enough the star ceases fusion reactions completely. The star's outer layers are shed and they expand out into space, while its core contracts to become an inert white dwarf with a diameter similar to Earth but with a mass generally between half and two-thirds of a solar mass . Therefore, the Welopō'ai system was once a triple system with two sun-like stars plus the red dwarf. Now the two sun-like stars have undergone this stage of star death while their companion red dwarf continues to linger, since its low mass bequeaths it a longer life because it does not use up its core hydrogen as quickly. One of the white dwarfs orbits the red dwarf at a distance of 129.3 astronomical units (19.3 billion kilometers or 12 billion miles) and takes about 1,000 years to complete one orbit. This white dwarf and the red dwarf were previously known, and Artigau's team had been using the SPectropolarimètre InfraROUge (SPIRou) instrument on the Canada–France–Hawaii Telescope atop Mauna Kea to search for planets orbiting the red dwarf when they noticed something highly unusual. Observations of the Welopō'ai triple-star system, located 28 light-years from Earth. The image on the left shows the two components of the system: Welopō'ai A, a closely orbiting red dwarf and white dwarf pair, and Welopō'ai B, a second white dwarf located much farther away. The image on the right provides a close-up view of the inner pair, revealing the faint white dwarf companion (Ab) detected using the Gemini North telescope's 'Alopeke instrument. The overlaid curves illustrate the stars'
item.dc:creator: Keith Cooper
item.content:encoded: A triple system containing a dim red dwarf star and not one but two white dwarfs has been fortuitously discovered just 28 light-years away from our solar system. "We were actually looking for planets ," Étienne Artigau of the Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets at the Université de Montréal, who led the discovery, said in a statement . "Instead, we found something much more surprising." So surprising that there are no similar systems within at least 100 light-years . Furthermore, the configuration of the system seems impossible. "This system should not exist," added Montreal's Patrick Dufour. "We have no clean explanation for how it got here." This triple system has been called Welopō'ai, which is a portmanteau of two Hawaiian words that means a 'path of family traits', and to understand the mystery behind it requires astronomers to figure out the history of the three objects. A white dwarf is what remains when a star of similar mass to our sun reaches the end of its life. As it begins to run low on hydrogen for nuclear fusion reactions in its core, the star's energy generation begins to falter and its interior starts to contract under gravity . This has the effect of raising the temperature throughout the star, causing an outer shell of hydrogen to ignite its own fusion reactions. The star promptly bloats to become a red giant tens or even hundreds of millions of kilometers across. Soon enough the star ceases fusion reactions completely. The star's outer layers are shed and they expand out into space, while its core contracts to become an inert white dwarf with a diameter similar to Earth but with a mass generally between half and two-thirds of a solar mass . Therefore, the Welopō'ai system was once a triple system with two sun-like stars plus the red dwarf. Now the two sun-like stars have undergone this stage of star death while their companion red dwarf continues to linger, since its low mass bequeaths it a longer life because it does not use up its core hydrogen as quickly. One of the white dwarfs orbits the red dwarf at a distance of 129.3 astronomical units (19.3 billion kilometers or 12 billion miles) and takes about 1,000 years to complete one orbit. This white dwarf and the red dwarf were previously known, and Artigau's team had been using the SPectropolarimètre InfraROUge (SPIRou) instrument on the Canada–France–Hawaii Telescope atop Mauna Kea to search for planets orbiting the red dwarf when they noticed something highly unusual. Observations of the Welopō'ai triple-star system, located 28 light-years from Earth. The image on the left shows the two components of the system: Welopō'ai A, a closely orbiting red dwarf and white dwarf pair, and Welopō'ai B, a second white dwarf located much farther away. The image on the right provides a close-up view of the inner pair, revealing the faint white dwarf companion (Ab) detected using the Gemini North telescope's 'Alopeke instrument. The overlaid curves illustrate the stars' orbital paths. (Image credit: Photo : Pan-STARRS1/STScI/MAST (left); International Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab (right). Graphic compilation: Étienne Artigau and Heidi White (UdeM/IREx)) SPIRou discovers planets by measuring how much their gravity tugs on their host star. Think of a star and planet orbiting a kind of gravitational balancing point between them called a center of mass. This center of mass is usually inside the star, since the star is far more massive than the planet, but crucially not at its very center, so the star appears to wobble to and fro around the combined center of mass. The spectrometer measures this wobble in the form of a Doppler shift in the star's light that can be translated into the velocity at which the star is moving around this center of mass. Astronomers call this a 'radial velocity'. A large gas giant like Jupiter might incur a radial velocity of hundreds of meters per second, while an Earth-mass planet generates a radial velocity of tens of meters. Yet the object that SPIRou found orbiting close to the red dwarf was creating a huge radial velocity signals of 10 miles (16 kilometers) per second. Whatever it was, it was not a planet. With the help of the eight-meter Gemini North telescope on Hawaii's Mauna Kea, Artigau's team were able to identify the mystery object as a white dwarf. "The unusual combination of high mass and very low brightness left only one plausible explanation: it was the remnant of a dead star," said Charles-Antoine Parent, an undergraduate student at Université Laval and a co-author of the study. White dwarfs are not exactly rare, and even finding two white dwarfs together is not unheard of: WD 0727+482 is a binary white dwarf system 37 light-years away, for example. To encounter two white dwarfs in a triple system with a regular star though is a precious find. The reason being that the masses of white dwarfs are not generally well defined. Yet their masses are not random; they are directly connected to the mass of the star that produced them. Thanks to the newly discovered white dwarf being separated from the red dwarf by about 4.6 astronomical units (688 million kilometers/428 million miles) – that's closer than Jupiter orbits our sun – Artigau's team were able to measure their masses to within an uncertainty of less than 1%. They found that the red dwarf has a mass 42% that of our sun and the newly discovered white dwarf has a mass 62% that of our sun. When the white dwarf was a regular star it would have had a mass 40% greater than our sun. The second more distant white dwarf orbits the pair of them. The Gemini North telescope in Hawaii, which helped identify the stars in the Welopō'ai triple system. (Image credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/J. Warner) The Welopō'ai system is therefore a good system for testing our models of stellar evolution that dictate how massive a white dwarf should be. If we know the white dwarf's mass with high precision, scientists can also use that as a starting point from which to explore the extreme physics of the white dwarf's condensed matter, which is being held up and prevented from contracting any further by something called electron degeneracy pressure – the unwillingness of negatively charged electrons to crush down any further and merge with positively charged protons to form neutrons . That takes the extra gravity from a more massive star to form a neutron star . So why should Welopō'ai not exist? The trouble is that when stars turn into red giants they really stir things up. Even if the red giant didn't expand out as far as the red dwarf, the expansion should have destabilized the red dwarf's orbit and potentially even caused it to crash into the red giant. Yet here the red dwarf is in a happily stable orbit like nothing had happened. "That is the question driving our next observations," said Dufour. It is hoped that further, more detailed, measurements of the gravitational interactions between the three members of the Welopō'ai system will help the team disentangle the evolutionary history of the trio to better understand their orbits and how the red dwarf survived. And because they are so relatively close to us, we have the advantage of being able to make high-precision measurements. "Discoveries like this remind us that our own cosmic neighborhood still contains remarkable surprises," said Artigau. "Even when we're searching for planets, our universe often has something completely unexpected waiting for us." The discovery of the Welopō'ai triple system is described in a paper published on Nov. 19 in Astronomy & Astrophysics .

item.title: From Mind Games to Ghost Stories! 5 Nollywood Titles to Stream This Week
item.description: Wande Thomas’s psychological thriller Spiraling, starring Toni Tones, Jim Iyke, Folu Storms and Seun Ajayi on KAVA, is among the titles recommended to watch this week. Wrongfully accused, caught in a web of lies, pulled into a dangerous family feud or haunted by a past you never saw coming. This week’s streaming picks have a little bit of everything for anyone who enjoys a story that refuses to let them relax. We’ve rounded up five titles across Circuits, Netflix, Prime Video and KAVA, taking you from psychological thrillers and gang conflicts to supernatural mysteries and a night out that spirals into something much bigger. Extra Mile — Circuits Sometimes trying to do a good deed for someone else is how everything goes sideways. That is the trap at the heart of this drama, where a woman ends up behind bars for a crime she never committed after stepping in to help a friend. Mercy Johnson – Okojie , Jim Iyke and Lilian Esoro carry the story forward under Kayode Kasum ‘s direction, working from a screenplay by Folasade Osibo and with Joy Grant – Ekong and Solate Ovundah – Akarolo on board as producers. Double Decoy — Circuits Moving from courtroom-style heartbreak straight into psychological mind games, our next pick on the same platform turns suspicion into a sport. Nothing looks straightforward when hidden agendas, shifting loyalties and high-stakes deception collide in this tense thriller. As every move feels like a test of trust, viewers are left guessing who is really pulling the strings, anchored by Kanayo O . Kanayo , Sola Sobowale and Gideon Okeke . Behind the scenes, the credits point to Oluwafemi Isaac Akinsipe alongside Nnamdi E . Odunze and Chichi Stylxz . The Covenant Season 2 — Netflix If that kind of high-stakes tension gets you in the mood for bigger battles and family rivalries, head over to Netflix next where the stakes climb even higher. Picking up right where the first run left off, the second season plunges deeper into power struggles, family loyalty and survival as Dagogo gets pulled further into dangerous conflicts and old scores. Gideon Okeke is back alongside Uzee Usman in a story created by Vincent Okonkwo and directed by Menelik Shabazz (“menelikfather”), mixing tense action, supernatural undertones and shifting alliances that keep the pressure on. Ajuwaya 2: Ghost of Selema — Prime Video Trading gang wars and big empires for eerie small-town secrets, our next stop on Prime Video shifts the tension somewhere much closer to home. Imagine posting up for youth service in a new town only to become the fixation of a troubled young man—and then digging into his past and finding a secret that links him straight to you with every reason to haunt you. Tolu LordTanner directs this suspenseful drama starring Godspower Nwogwugwu , Damilola Onitilo , Oyeyemi Adeoye and Ovy Godwin . item.title: Solape Fayemi Launches Saina Properties Across Four Markets
item.description: For many people, buying property is one of the biggest financial decisions they will ever make. Yet, knowing who to trust, how to verify ownership and whether a property is worth the investment can make the process overwhelming. It is a challenge Solape Fayemi hopes to address with the launch of Saina Properties , a real estate company now operating across Nigeria, the United Kingdom, the United States and the United Arab Emirates. Officially unveiled at an event held on 17 November at the Marriott Hotel, Ikeja GRA, Lagos, Saina Properties is built around a simple idea: property ownership should be guided by sound advice, proper verification and professional support, not just the excitement of closing a deal. For Solape, whose experience in the investment industry shaped her understanding of money, risk and wealth creation, the decision to establish the company came from recognising the need for a more considered approach to real estate. “We are not building Saina Properties because the world needs another company selling properties. We are building Saina because we believe there is room for a different kind of real estate experience. One where advice comes before the transaction, where due diligence is not treated as an inconvenience, and where people are encouraged to ask questions, understand their options and make informed decisions,” she said at the launch. That philosophy is reflected in the company’s three core areas of expertise: Advisory & Verification, Sales & Brokerage, and Developments . Rather than focusing solely on connecting buyers to properties, Saina brings together the guidance investors need to assess opportunities, the support required to navigate property transactions, and involvement in real estate development. The company is also building on experience gained before its official launch, having supported more than 25 clients with property opportunities across different markets. An important part of its proposition is the role of professional expertise in protecting property investors. Fayemi’s position raises a familiar question: people consult doctors for medical concerns and lawyers for legal matters, so why do some investors leave significant property decisions in the hands of relatives simply because they are available or familiar with the location? While trust and family relationships matter, they do not automatically translate into the technical knowledge needed to assess a property, verify its documentation or understand its investment potential. These decisions require proper checks, market understanding and accountability. With its operations spanning four markets, Saina Properties aims to support individuals and investors looking to navigate property ownership with greater clarity, whether they are buying, selling or exploring development opportunities. Its guiding promise captures the thinking behind the business: “ With Saina Properties, you own with certainty.” Solape Fayemi is the Chief Executive Officer of Sa

Drawing on her experience in the investment industry, Solape brings a strong understanding of wealth creation, risk management, and capital preservation to her approach to real estate. Under her leadership, Saina Properties is focused on making property ownership a more informed and transparent experience, built on professional guidance, due diligence and long-term client relationships. item.title: Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action
item.description: Leeds offer Chelsea a lesson, Newcastle’s summer recruits struggle and Jules Ahoka makes a name for himself What to make of Manchester United’s utterly torrid start under Mauricio Pochettino? To go glass half full as the new head coach had only three days to prepare the side for the trip to Anfield, the hope will be that time will cast the 4-0 humbling from Liverpool as the falsest of false starts. The glass-half-empty scenario, though, is that here was an XI packed with internationals that had zero clue how to sort out a dire beginning themselves. Leny Yoro’s very early red card may have been questionable but for the wall to evaporate and allow Dominik Szoboszlai’s subsequent free-kick to arrow home was damning evidence of how immature Pochettino’s new charges are. From here it became a debacle and the players, if they have anything about them, need to apologise to the head coach, hold a meeting between themselves and demand they start taking responsibility. If not, United are heading only one way: down. Jamie Jackson Match report: Liverpool 4-0 Manchester United ‘It’s painful for me’: Pochettino criticises Yoro red card decision Continue reading...

item.title: How Mary Akinwola Graduated with a Distinction from Oxford After Receiving Multiple Scholarships
item.description: Mary Akinwola graduated from the University of Oxford after receiving the Chevening and Mastercard Foundation Scholarships. My name is Mary Akinwola. I’m a physiotherapist, a strategy consultant, a healthcare entrepreneur, and I recently graduated from the University of Oxford with a distinction in Health Service Improvement and Evaluation. I have probably said that last part a hundred times since getting my results, and honestly, I don’t think I’m tired of saying it yet. Haha! One thing about me is that I like to be involved. I am sometimes curious about things that have absolutely nothing to do with what I’m supposed to be doing, and I genuinely enjoy working with people. I like organising things, bringing people together, and seeing an idea move forward to get accomplished. So I have known that going to Oxford was never going to be just about getting a master’s degree. Let me explain how I ended up there. I studied Physiotherapy at the University of Ibadan, where I graduated with First-Class Honours. During my undergraduate years, I was involved in quite a lot outside academics: student leadership, journalism, research, community health programmes and advocacy. My involvement in community health exposed me to how differently people experience healthcare depending on where they live, what they can afford and what information they have access to. I loved being a physiotherapist, and that allowed me to interrogate questions that went beyond individual patient care. Why do some people receive good healthcare while others struggle to access even basic services? How do we make healthcare more affordable? What role can technology play? And why do some seemingly good healthcare programmes struggle to produce lasting change? Eventually, I realised I wanted to study and work in a field that constantly seeks to improve health systems. I researched different programmes across the US and UK, hoping to study at institutions that have international audiences where I could build a diverse perspective in health. I came across the MSc in Health Service Improvement and Evaluation at the University of Oxford’s Nuffield Department of Medicine. It aligned with many of my interests, so I applied. I also needed a scholarship because, quite frankly, I couldn’t afford Oxford. It was a humbling and affirming process. I was awarded scholarships such as the Chevening Scholarship and two Oxford-based scholarships. I still feel fortunate to have received and chosen the Mastercard Foundation-Africa Oxford Initiative Scholarship, which fully funded my studies. I am deeply grateful for that opportunity. Now, I think it’s important to say that I was very excited about the academic programme. I wanted to understand healthcare systems better, learn new research methods and become more effective at designing and evaluating healthcare services. However, I was also very excited about everything else. I was going to be at Oxford! There were going to be people from different countries
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija Features
item.content:encoded: Mary Akinwola graduated from the University of Oxford after receiving the Chevening and Mastercard Foundation Scholarships. My name is Mary Akinwola. I’m a physiotherapist, a strategy consultant, a healthcare entrepreneur, and I recently graduated from the University of Oxford with a distinction in Health Service Improvement and Evaluation. I have probably said that last part a hundred times since getting my results, and honestly, I don’t think I’m tired of saying it yet. Haha! One thing about me is that I like to be involved. I am sometimes curious about things that have absolutely nothing to do with what I’m supposed to be doing, and I genuinely enjoy working with people. I like organising things, bringing people together, and seeing an idea move forward to get accomplished. So I have known that going to Oxford was never going to be just about getting a master’s degree. Let me explain how I ended up there. I studied Physiotherapy at the University of Ibadan, where I graduated with First-Class Honours. During my undergraduate years, I was involved in quite a lot outside academics: student leadership, journalism, research, community health programmes and advocacy. My involvement in community health exposed me to how differently people experience healthcare depending on where they live, what they can afford and what information they have access to. I loved being a physiotherapist, and that allowed me to interrogate questions that went beyond individual patient care. Why do some people receive good healthcare while others struggle to access even basic services? How do we make healthcare more affordable? What role can technology play? And why do some seemingly good healthcare programmes struggle to produce lasting change? Eventually, I realised I wanted to study and work in a field that constantly seeks to improve health systems. I researched different programmes across the US and UK, hoping to study at institutions that have international audiences where I could build a diverse perspective in health. I came across the MSc in Health Service Improvement and Evaluation at the University of Oxford’s Nuffield Department of Medicine. It aligned with many of my interests, so I applied. I also needed a scholarship because, quite frankly, I couldn’t afford Oxford. It was a humbling and affirming process. I was awarded scholarships such as the Chevening Scholarship and two Oxford-based scholarships. I still feel fortunate to have received and chosen the Mastercard Foundation-Africa Oxford Initiative Scholarship, which fully funded my studies. I am deeply grateful for that opportunity. Now, I think it’s important to say that I was very excited about the academic programme. I wanted to understand healthcare systems better, learn new research methods and become more effective at designing and evaluating healthcare services. However, I was also very excited about everything else. I was going to be at Oxford! There were going to be people from different countries, lectures, events, societies, research opportunities, interesting conversations, and all sorts of things I didn’t even know existed yet. I wanted to experience as much of it as possible. One of the first things I realised was how much to learn from other people. My classmates came from different professional and geographical backgrounds, and our conversations were often as interesting as the lectures themselves. Someone would describe how healthcare worked in their country, and I’d realise that something I had always assumed was normal was actually quite specific to my own experience. Or we’d discuss a health systems problem, and someone would approach it in a way I hadn’t considered. I loved that. I also found the academic programme quite demanding when we were introduced to unfamiliar methods or theories. There were times when I had to sit with an idea for a while before it made sense, but I enjoyed being challenged, and I had wonderful classmates and teachers to learn from. The lectures and lecturers were very interactive and creative in their approach to imparting knowledge. I am still inspired by their methods and hope to collaborate with the program someday. Outside the classroom, I did what I usually do: I found things to get involved in. I became Class Representative for my cohort, worked on consulting projects with the University of Oxford’s Making a Difference Program and the Oxford Strategy Group, joined the Skoll Centre Impact Lab, and attended the Skoll World Forum. I participated in the BCG-Oxford Africa Case Competition, where my team emerged as first runner-up. I presented research at academic conferences, received a presentation prize, and helped lead an Innovation Seed Fund programme which supported 4 African teams with funding and readiness support. Gleaning from the creative approach applied in my lectures, I also co-organised a simulation workshop marking the tenth anniversary of the Africa Oxford Initiative with some of my closest friends (Amina, Farida and Lydia). Sometimes, I had several commitments happening around the same period, and I had to figure out how to make everything work. I had to up time management and I also learned to say no in many cases. I genuinely enjoyed everything I did. I wasn’t doing these things just to have something to put on my CV. I liked the people I was meeting, the problems we were trying to solve, and the opportunity to try my hand at different things. The funniest part is that, towards the end of the programme, my classmates and teaching staff voted me “Extracurricular Legend.” I laughed so much when I got up to collect the award. Apparently, I had developed a reputation for being involved in everything. Naija no dey carry last sha. I think what made my time at Oxford special, though, was the people. I met some wonderfully brilliant, generous and interesting people. I had conversations that made me question things I’d always believed, and others that were just completely unserious. I built friendships that I really hope will last for years. I felt comfortable expressing myself, asking questions, trying new things and sometimes just admitting that I didn’t know something. When you spend a lot of time working towards particular goals, it can be easy to think about your life in terms of what you need to achieve next. Get the degree. Secure the opportunity. Build the company. Make the next move. I am still very ambitious, and I don’t think that’s going to change, but I also really enjoyed being where I was. I enjoyed learning simply because something was interesting. I enjoyed discovering new places, meeting people, spending time with my friends and participating in activities that had nothing to do with my career. It felt like such a complete year, and then I graduated with a distinction! I was so happy. I had worked hard academically, and it was wonderful to see that reflected in my results, but I was also proud that I had made so much of the wider experience. Someone described Oxford as the most flower-like season, and I know that’s a slightly unusual description, but it really is how I feel. I bloomed, really. My family has been happy about the graduation, and that means a lot to me. My mum is a physiotherapist, and she has been an enormous influence on my life. Growing up, I watched her work very hard to provide for my siblings and me and ensure we received a good education. She made considerable sacrifices, and I am very grateful to her. I sometimes think about the little girl who followed her mum to work and spent hours reading whatever medical books she could find. I don’t think she would have predicted this particular chapter of her life. I am grateful to the Mastercard Foundation, the Africa Oxford Initiative, my lecturers, my friends, St Peter’s College, my mentors and everyone who helped make my Oxford experience what it was. I am excited about working with organisations that drive change, especially in heal

item.title: Zadok Is Singing About Finding Real Love in His New Single “My Treasure”
item.description: Zadok Aghalengbe drops his new single “My Treasure”, an Afro-fusion, R&B and soul love song. In the mood for a love song that makes you appreciate having that special someone in your life? Zadok Aghalengbe has something new for your playlist. The Nigerian singer and songwriter, who finished as runner-up on Nigerian Idol Season 7, has dropped “My Treasure”, a new single all about love, gratitude and holding on to someone worth keeping. Pulling together Afro-fusion, contemporary R&B and soul, the track puts Zadok’s rich, husky vocals front and centre over a story of devotion and real connection. Dubbed the “Preacher of Love”, he keeps leaning into romantic themes in his music, with “My Treasure” showing his push to make love songs that last. Speaking about the inspiration behind the record, Zadok describes it as a celebration of finding something rare and genuine. He also hopes the song captures the gratitude and connection that come with having someone truly special. Listen below ﻿ The post Zadok Is Singing About Finding Real Love in His New Single “My Treasure” appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: “Money in a Wheelbarrow”: Adekunle Gold & Blaqbonez Are Making Big-Money Talk Sound Good
item.description: Artwork for Adekunle Gold and Blaqbonez’s collaboration “Money in a Wheelbarrow”. Did you ever envisage an Adekunle Gold and Blaqbonez collaboration? You’re not alone, neither did we, but as it turns out, “ Money in a Wheelbarrow ” is officially here—and Adekunle Gold shared that this is actually a link-up with an artist who released a diss track about him years ago, plus their second attempt at making a song together. If you enjoy a track with a cheeky backstory behind it, this one is all about celebrating your hard-earned bag, enjoying the fruits of your grind and soaking up good moments right now instead of putting joy off until later. On the song itself, Adekunle Gold brings his smooth, melodic touch alongside Blaqbonez’s witty rap delivery as they trade lines about stacking cash, containers landing in Apapa and living large. You get a lively mix of English, Nigerian Pidgin and Yoruba phrasing that makes you want to sing along fast, turning big-money talk into something bright and upbeat rather than heavy. The visuals match that playful mood right from the start, with bold pixel-style lettering flashing across the screen over a bright backdrop where both artists are dressed in sharp dark suits, ties, sunglasses and stacks of cash. Watching them pose around wheelbarrows piled with money as words like “Wheel Barrow”, “Pack Am O”, “Container”, “Apapa”, “Hosana” and “Duffel Bag” pop up gives the video a fun, tongue-in-cheek edge that keeps your eyes locked on the screen. I f you want a fresh, upbeat tune with a funny plot twist behind it, “Money in a Wheelbarrow” is ready for your playlist. *** Photo Credit: Adekunle Gold/Instagram The post “Money in a Wheelbarrow”: Adekunle Gold & Blaqbonez Are Making Big-Money Talk Sound Good appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Rema & Wizkid Have Us Singing Along to “Feel Alright” With This New Lyric Video
item.description: Scene from the official lyric video for Rema and Wizkid’s “Feel Alright” off the seven-track EP E-Mortal Boy (EMB). If you have been singing along to “ Feel Alright ” since E-Mortal Boy came out, Rema has just dropped the official lyric video so you can finally catch every single line without guessing. Having the words on screen makes it much easier to follow how Rema and Wizkid trade verses on the opening track, mixing smooth R&B-leaning melodies with English, Nigerian Pidgin and Yoruba slang as they serenade a love interest. For plenty of listeners, “Feel Alright” is the biggest talking point on E-Mortal Boy because it marks the very first official collaboration between Rema and Wizkid, bringing two distinct Afrobeats eras together right at the start of the project. Putting out a lyric video for the track gives fans of both artists a chance to properly take in the lyrics and harmonies that have had the song on heavy rotation since the project landed. The release also keeps the spotlight on E-Mortal Boy, Rema’s seven-track EP that followed earlier singles “TEA” and “Oh No”. Alongside “Feel Alright” with Wizkid, the project includes “Velvet”, “TANZANIA” with BNYX, “SUGA” with Theodora , and closer “Bang Bang” with London and Kah-Lo , showing off the wide range of sounds Rema pulls together across the seven songs. If you have been waiting to learn every word of Rema and Wizkid’s first joint record, this lyric video has you covered. item.title: The Wedding Countdown Is On! Diana Eneje & Pascal Godwin Celebrate Their Introduction in Royal Blue
item.description: Pascal Godwin in Rogue and Diana Eneje in Dova Bridals at their introduction ceremony, styled by Emmanuel Goodnews Icon. Diana Eneje and Pascal Godwin ‘s forever journey has begun, but first of all, introductions! Three months after Pascal proposed against the backdrop of Cape Town’s mountains and vineyards in August 2026, the Nigerian fashion influencer and entrepreneur and her Lagos-based businessman fiancé have taken another lovely step towards walking down the aisle. While they are not married just yet, the couple have officially held their introduction ceremony, bringing both families together ahead of their traditional and white weddings. For anyone unfamiliar with the tradition, the introduction is an important first step in many Nigerian weddings. It is when the couple’s families meet formally, exchange greetings, offer prayers and give their blessings as the relationship moves towards marriage. And while the main wedding celebrations are still ahead, Diana and Pascal have given us a first look at what we can expect from their wedding style. Diana Eneje and Pascal Godwin in coordinated royal blue looks by Dova Bridals and Rogue for their introduction ceremony. If you’ve followed Diana from her early modelling days and her appearance in Rema ‘s 2019 “ Dumebi ” music video to building her beauty brand, The Shine Cartel, you’ll know that fashion is always part of her story. Styled together by Emmanuel Goodnews Icon , the two stepped out in coordinated royal blue looks, with Dova Bridals creating Diana’s introduction dress that brought together lace, colourful woven fabric and satin. Diana Eneje wearing a custom royal blue beaded lace, woven fabric, and satin mermaid gown by Dova Bridals. Her dress featured an off-the-shoulder beaded lace bodice with a sweetheart neckline and short tiered sleeves. From the waist, it flowed into a chevron-patterned woven skirt featuring shades of red, green, gold and blue, before opening into a pleated royal blue satin mermaid hem. She completed the look with a matching beaded fan handbag, silver jewellery with dark stone accents and crystal-strapped blue heels, alongside a sleek updo with sculpted waves. Diana Eneje in her custom Dova Bridals royal blue beaded lace and woven introduction dress, styled by Emmanuel Goodnews Icon and photographed by Chuchu Ojekwe Pascal coordinated with Diana in a custom royal blue velvet traditional robe and trouser set by Rogue . Gold and silver geometric and botanical beadwork ran across the chest, shoulders and sleeves, continuing down to the fringed hem . He finished with a matching beaded cap, layered deep blue beads and a gold pendant, dark-tinted sunglasses, a gold wristwatch and dark velvet loafers, with a tall carved black walking staff completing his traditional look . Pascal Godwin in a custom royal blue velvet traditional outfit by Rogue, styled by Emmanuel Goodnews Icon and photographed by Chuchu Ojekwe With the introduction ceremony behind them, Diana and Pascal’s

item.title: Elizabeth Agboola: Your Next Flight From Nigeria Could Be Two Holidays in One. Here’s How
item.description: Have you ever spent six hours in an airport waiting for your connecting flight, watching the departure screens, browsing duty-free shops and wondering what the city outside looks like? Perhaps you were connecting through Istanbul, Doha, Dubai or Addis Ababa. You were technically in another country, but the closest you came to experiencing it was buying a souvenir at the airport. What if I told you that some airlines could help you turn that connection into an additional holiday, sometimes even providing accommodation? Having travelled to more than 70 countries, I have learnt that one of the smartest ways to travel is to pay attention to the journey, not just the destination. Many Nigerians book international tickets based on price, travel time and baggage allowance. These are important considerations, but there is another question worth asking: What else can this ticket give me? I am talking about stopovers, not the hurried two-hour connection where you are running between terminals, but an intentional break in your journey that allows you to experience another destination before continuing to the country you originally planned to visit. And with the right airline, itinerary and travel documents, that additional experience might cost less than you imagine. First, Understand What You Are Booking A layover is generally a connection between flights; a stopover is a longer, planned break in your journey. Airlines define these differently, and the distinction matters because some offer special hotel packages, sightseeing tours or complimentary accommodation to qualifying passengers. For example, imagine travelling from Lagos to London through Istanbul. Instead of spending a few hours at Istanbul Airport, you could investigate whether your ticket qualifies for a longer stopover, allowing you to explore Istanbul before continuing to London. You have now turned one international journey into an opportunity to experience two destinations outside Nigeria. The secret is to investigate the stopover before purchasing your ticket, rather than arriving at the airport and hoping the airline will allow you to stay longer. For visa purposes, Nigerians do not qualify, but with a valid Turkish visa you would be able to qualify for some of the perks. Under the standard programme, eligible Economy Class passengers can receive one night in a four-star hotel, while Business Class passengers may receive two nights in a five-star or boutique hotel.
